This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Thanksgiving is nearly upon us and, with that, avid TV viewers can look forward to plenty of programming specifically geared towards the holiday. As all of those special offerings roll in on network TV, some may be wondering what’s going on with the late-night shows. There are now details regarding what hosts Jimmy Fallon, Jimmy Kimmel and Seth Meyers have planned for this coming week. And, from the looks of it, Fallon is differentiating himself from Kimmel over the holidays in a very keen way.

NBC – which houses both The Tonight Show and Late Night with Seth Meyers – has long capitalized on Turkey Day. After all, the storied network remains the home of the beloved Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade (which Fallon has participated in). Historically, Fallon and Meyers’ shows have sought to draw in viewers even on the night of the holiday, and that’ll continue this year. Both shows will be on for T-giving amid the 2026 TV schedule, and they have some special developments planned.

Per NBC’s press site, Fallon’s Tonight Show will kick off the week of November 23 with a repeat on Monday and then run new episodes from Tuesday to Thursday. When it comes to the Thanksgiving broadcast, Fallon is set to welcome back his old pal, Justin Timberlake, to the show for the first time in two years. Said episode could lead to some memorable moments as has been the case with past T-giving broadcasts. I’m sure some devoted viewers remember Fallon and Kevin James’ messy food sketch from 2016.

Meanwhile, Seth Meyers’ Late Night will drop new episodes from Monday, November 23 through Thursday November 26. And, for the holiday, Meyers is continuing his tradition of having his family members on the show for Thanksgiving. Amy Poehler and Tina Fey – Meyers’ longtime friends from his SNL days – will also appear during that holiday show.

It definitely tracks that NBC would want to keep these late-night offerings on the air during Thanksgiving. Not only networks are alike, though, as it seems that Jimmy Kimmel and co. at ABC are going a different route.

The ABC press site confirms that Jimmy Kimmel Live! will only air new episodes on Monday, November 23 and Tuesday, November 24. For the remainder of the week, the show will go on a break and reruns will air in its place. So, in other words, this marks a brief hiatus for the team over at Live! Of course, such a break isn’t unheard of for this show or any other like it. What’s also worth noting is that this break comes months after Kimmel’s latest time away from the desk.

Over the summer, Kimmel took some time off, and that’s something he’s done over the past several years. During that time, his show remains on the air, though, and a cavalcade of guest hosts are brought in each week until Kimmel returns. Those guest host stints can be quite eventful (as viewers learned when Tiffany Haddish hosted back in July).

When it comes to these Thanksgiving strategies, though, there definitely doesn’t seem to be anything too out of the ordinary. Jimmy Kimmel’s show can also seemingly afford to take a little time off, given the show has been crushing in the ratings, especially in the aftermath of The Late Show’s cancellation. (We’ll tear off a drumstick in your honor, Stephen Colbert.) All in all, though, I’m interested in seeing what Jimmy Fallon’s The Tonight Show and Seth Meyers’ Late Night offer on T-giving as well as how they end up doing viewership-wise.

#3429. Blade Runner 2099 Review: Hunter Schafer And Michelle Yeoh Star In The Best Sci-Fi Show In Years

In the case of the "Blade Runner" franchise, the future seems to arrive right on time. It's no coincidence that both films in the series were made during periods of severe social and political anxiety in America, with their dystopias not just predicting our future but reflecting our present. Although Ridley Scott's 1982 masterpiece is still generally well regarded, it also feels a little underrated in terms of how massively influential it was. It not only still casts a shadow over the science fiction genre, but began a trend within Hollywood of more filmmakers utilizing the works of author Philip K. Dick, whose novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" served as the source material. It was instrumental in kicking off the cyberpunk subgenre, with so many tech-centric dystopias following in its wake. Meanwhile, Denis Villeneuve's decades-later sequel "Blade Runner 2049" is a masterwork in its own right, a sequel which has itself inspired pop culture.

As we endure this latest period of anxiety, along comes a new "Blade Runner" to mirror our malaise. We're in a particularly fertile period for dark sci-fi to emerge, with everything from the rise of AI to the failure of governmental and technical systems occurring around us. As such, it feels fitting that this new "Blade Runner" isn't another movie, but an 8-episode series: "Blade Runner 2099." As the title suggests, this isn't some lazy continuation, but is instead a leap forward within the series' parallel universe in which artificial humans known as Replicants exist. Showrunner Silka Luisa has put together something that's as unique and bold as it is in conversation with its franchise's past, making it a proud new addition to the saga. In many ways, "Blade Runner 2099" is the best sci-fi show in years.

"Blade Runner 2099" introduces us to the surprisingly sunny but still noir-ish Los Angeles of 2099, a city which feels like Ridley Scott's overcrowded metropolis and Denis Villeneuve's stark landscapes have been merged. More than just paying homage to the past, this provides a fitting backdrop to an LA which exists after the Replicant uprising (which was hinted at toward the end of "2049"). Now the script has been flipped: Replicants are the dominant species on Earth, having subjugated the remaining humans. Those humans who cannot go (or are not sent) off-world occupy menial jobs, and any who exhibit resistance are retired by Replicant Blade Runners.

After the human Cora (Hunter Schafer) gets caught in a Blade Runner raid at her job where she's forced to run, she tries to use a human sympathizer, Bebeto (Dimitri Abold) to help her and her disabled brother Elias (Lewis Gribben) get to Mexico City, the last city on Earth where humanity has true freedom. Bebeto needs Cora to do something for him in exchange, which is to pose as a Replicant (and a Blade Runner) in order to obtain an object from LAPD lockup.

Upon attempting this, Cora is suddenly assigned to work with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a veteran Blade Runner whose predetermined Replicant death time is coming up shortly. With that, the series is off on its own unique sci-fi/noir trip. While there are several callbacks to prior elements of the franchise (things like the Voight-Kampff test and the JOI device make an appearance), these are part of its worldbuilding more than any fan service. "2099" is unquestionably a part of "Blade Runner," yet its reconfiguring of the world allows it to stand alone, too.

Right away, the franchise's themes of identity, existentialism, and morality come to the fore in the series, all of which showrunner Silka Luisa and company explore with aplomb. A big part of why it feels so fresh lies in the show's female leads, a development which feels natural rather than belabored.

Though the themes of "Blade Runner" have always been universal, the first two films do have notably masculine viewpoints. Here, Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh bring a new feminine energy to the franchise which feels distinct from the men in the franchise but also from the previous films' women. Yeoh's extensive history with the action genre makes Olwen's strength almost second nature, while Schafer builds upon her excellent work in "Cuckoo" by making Cora a woman who is also slowly getting more and more in over her head. These layered characterizations are helped by the series' scripts, which are of a idiosyncratic, sci-fi-forward quality worthy of the franchise.

As great as the performances and writing are, the folks behind "Blade Runner 2099" are well aware that a large part of the series' fame is due to its visual design, and as such the series has not skimped in that department. "2099" utilizes its status as a series to take us to many more places in the "Blade Runner" universe than just LA and the surrounding areas, and the production design goes beyond Scott and Villeneuve as influences. In fact, one sequence feels worthy of mentioning in the same breath as Andrei Tarkovsky. Meanwhile, the series' cinematographers (led by Rob Hardy) maintain a consistently strong level of quality over the episodes, while composer Leopold Ross builds a hypnotically strange sonic tapestry that never reuses old themes.

"Blade Runner 2099" is one of those shows that leaves you awed at how they managed to accomplish so much with it. If there is a flaw within, it's the usual issue with so many streaming series these days, which is that some story beats (and a few whole scenes) feel unnecessarily lengthened and padded out. It's also a shame that Prime Video is releasing the show all at once, as it feels like the series was produced to foster a week-to-week audience (similar to "Crystal Lake" from last month), and, given its rich material, could've likely grown one. That aside, "Blade Runner 2099" is a show that has a lot going for it, not the least of which is its intelligence and imagination.

It carries on the concepts and themes of Philip K. Dick while adding some wild new ideas. Its closest cousin in this way may be another Ridley Scott-backed series, the underseen "Raised By Wolves." Given its boldness, one wonders if the 8 episodes of "2099" are intended as the final word, both for itself and for "Blade Runner" in general. Whatever the future holds, I believe the show is the best sci-fi IP revival since Ronald D. Moore's "Battlestar Galactica." It's that intriguing, that layered, and that vibrant. In keeping with the original film's reputation, the various interpretations that the series' ending invites are enough to keep the show worth talking about for years to come. It may have been almost a decade since "2049," but "Blade Runner 2099" has arrived right on time.

"Blade Runner 2099" premieres November 25, 2026 on Prime Video.

#3428. Boy Was ‘Begging for His Life’ Before Father Killed Family in Murder-Suicide

Authorities in Florida revealed additional heartbreaking details of a 911 call before a father killed his wife and three young children in a murder-suicide.

The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office confirmed that Isaac Luechtefeld, and his wife, Raquel Luechtefeld, were found dead alongside their children, Enoch, 5, Hannah, 3, and Job, 1, at their home in Plant City, Florida, on Thursday, November 19.

Investigators said they believe Isaac, 34, fatally shot his family inside their home before he died by suicide.

Dispatchers received a 911 call from the home around 3:30 p.m. on Thursday and reported hearing gunshots in the background.

“It’s an open line, and we can hear a male’s voice say, ‘Sorry, buddy.’ And we hear a loud bang,” Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister said during a news conference on Thursday.

An open-line call connects to 911 without the caller speaking, which allows dispatchers to hear background noises.

“In the distance, we can hear a small child begging for his life,” Chronister continued.

The child was then heard begging his father to spare his life. “Daddy, please don’t shoot me. Daddy, please don’t kill me,” the sheriff said of the child’s pleas.

Chronister said that the child repeated the pleas three or four times before dispatchers said they heard another loud bang.

Deputies arrived at the home just 11 minutes after the 911 call came through at 3:40 p.m. Once they got to the home, officers spotted one of the children lying lifeless on the floor and they forced their way into the residence.

Chronister went on to say that all five family members were found dead with gunshot wounds.

“When you become a deputy sheriff, you expect to see awful things, but what the deputies encountered here today is nothing short of pure evil,” Chronister added.

Despite confirming details of the horrific killings, Chronister did not state if authorities have established a motive. He also said that they are still trying to figure out what incidents led up to the murder-suicide.

Many of the first responders and the 911 dispatcher were left in shock over the killings, and they were required to “take a time out.” Those employees were also connected with the department’s peer support team and were given other resources to help them process the tragedy.

“There are no words that can capture the depth of this tragedy,” Chronister said in a press release when the sheriff’s office first announced the murder-suicice “A family has been lost, and our hearts are with their loved ones, friends, and everyone in our community who knew them.”

#3427. The Method-Dressing Madness Behind Mckenna Grace‘s 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Press Tour Looks

Before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances. Made a household term by Law Roach and Zendaya, method dressing is when actors wear looks that pay homage to the film or show they’re promoting: See Zendaya’s on-theme looks across red carpets for Dune, Spiderman, and The Odyssey for a slew of examples.

With the new Hunger Games film, it’s Grace’s turn to adopt the trend. A super fan of the Suzanne Collins book series and their film adaptations, Grace—who plays District 12 tribute Maysilee Donner—took a hand in the styling for her press run, weaving easter eggs into every look. Her stylist, Molly Dickson, was up for the challenge of translating Grace’s deep-cut references into custom and archival looks from Monique Lhuillier, Gucci, Celine and more.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.

Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

Molly Dickson: I went to college in Minnesota and my major was advertising. Two weeks before I graduated, I called my mom and said, "I'm not into this. I don't wanna do advertising." She said, "Well, what do you wanna do?" I told her, "I wanna do fashion. I wanna go to New York." She said, "No, absolutely not."

Right after I graduated, I went to LA, this was 2009 during the recession, and no one was hiring. I got an internship at Marie Claire in New York, and enrolled back into college to get school credit to intern at Hearst. I worked at Marie Claire as a market assistant for almost two years, and then I left and assisted Leslie Fremar for seven years. That's when I fell in love with celebrity. Then ten years ago, I went off on my own.

What would you say are your aesthetic influences as a stylist?

My personal style relates very similarly to Sadie Sink's style, very effortless. She always wants to be very comfortable and easy, never anything frilly or over the top. Just a simple, beautiful dress, and you let it speak for itself.

Mckenna is a big fan of the original film series, so it’s clear you’re pulling from there as influences when dressing her. Is it a collaborative process when coming to one of these referential looks?

She's obviously a very huge fan of the franchise. We actually started having conversations about this tour in April, which is very early to start having conversations. I could just sense her excitement around it. She started sending me mood boards, and I actually looked back today at the mood board and it was, it was a lot of Katniss Everdeen. It had Joanna on it, and it was filled with these really strong female characters from the franchise.

What she really wanted to hit was Katniss’ wedding gown look and the Mockingjay look with the wings. I was really stumped on how to pull that off without making it overly costumey.

Mckenna kept asking, "What's going on with those?" I knew the vision, but I didn't know how to execute it. I was working with Keke Palmer and the designer Michael Ngo. He was making some cool music costumes for Keke, and I asked, "Michael, could you make this silver piece?" 'Cause I really had no idea how to get it done.

He said, “I don't think I can do that. You know what? Just give me a day, let me play around with it." That night, he said, "I figured it out." We got the piece and I thought, "Okay, it needs to be a wedding dress under,” so I reached out to all the bridal houses. I wanted it to be vintage because it would tell a pretty story. Monique [Lhuillier] ended up sending a ton of wedding gowns, and the day before Mckenna came in for the fitting, I actually tried the wedding dresses on myself with the silver piece.

I sent Mckenna five dresses, and the one that she ended up wearing, she said, "That's it. I don't even need to try anything else. That's the one I'm gonna wear." Then, it was a matter of finding the right event to wear it to because it’s pretty nice, very dramatic.

She was in Paris for the Miu Miu show, and I brought it there because she had the Hunger Games Museum event. It was a whole conversation with her team, like, "Is it the right moment? Is it too much for this event?" Her PR said, "No, this is the perfect moment. It's the best way to kick off the tour." The response with the Hunger Games fans—I have never seen anything like it before, ever.

What was the experience of having her be such a big part of the styling process?

It makes my job so fun because she is so passionate about it and she loves Hunger Games so much, even just finding subtle nods back to the movie. She would say, "I wanna do a ladybug look." Thom Browne did that amazing ladybug dress, I thought, "That's so cool, but it's not really her personal aesthetic." So it’s finding ways to keep it still true to her personal style while maintaining the nods to the film.

The way you seem to understand Mckenna feels something similar to the connection between Katniss and Cinna in The Hunger Games. When pulling looks for her, what comes into play? How do you make her come through and not be lost in the lore of the stories or the dress?

Mckenna had said that she maybe wanted to do a red or a dark pink feather look because in the books [Maysilee] gets attacked by the red birds which are like flamingos. I'm pulling in all these red feather dresses and on the runway, this one dress looked amazing. Mckenna said, “That's perfect for the flamingo reference.”

But we put it on her and it was so big, and she's so petite so she was just getting swarmed. I said, “Let"s not force it.” The goal was for her to feel comfortable in the look rather than just getting each reference.

The public has been really excited about these looks. Are you thinking about the response to the looks when you’re putting them together?

There's been some conversations in a fitting, like, "Oh, the Hunger Games fans are gonna get this." They're gonna see the inspiration, they're gonna understand it.

But I wouldn't say we're choosing a look because ‘Oh, this is gonna go viral to the Hunger Games community.’ Mckenna is a super fan herself so if she's getting excited about the look, everyone else that's a fan of the franchise is gonna get excited about the look.

Do you feel any pressure to top the last outfit after each premiere?

Yes. I think it was Paris because that wedding dress did get so much press. In that fitting, it felt like, "We gotta keep our game up high." It's been really fun for my team and market assistants because a lot of the girls that work with me are huge fans of the movie. They're not even seeing it as work. They're like, "Oh my God, this is so exciting. Look at this. This looks like this from the movie."

What was the inspiration to do method dressing for this press run? What do you think is the value?

Mckenna knew back in April, she said, "I wanna do method for this." I personally did not read the books. I'm a visual person, so I've seen all the movies. Lionsgate was able to let me go with the cast when they first saw the movie because my agent was like, "Molly needs to go to the movie to get inspired before this press tour. She can't do a method dressing press tour without seeing the movie."

Even as the tour was going on, Mckenna kept sending me new references and quotes from the book and stuff like that.

What made you take it to the next level? From paying homage to not only characters, but the actual actors from the films like Jennifer Lawrence at the 2011 Oscars to even dressing like set pieces from the film.

That was all Mckenna's vision. On her first mood board, she had a lot of Jennifer Lawrence's red carpet moments because she's such a huge fan of Katniss and Jennifer Lawrence.

With the Rue reference, Mckenna thought that color was just very Hunger Games. It wasn't until she put the dress on, her mom said, "Wait, this is Rue's dress." So that was just fate. I would love to take credit for that.

Why do you think that this styling has generated so much attention?

I think it’s when you do method dressing for such a big franchise and you really are passionate about it. The thing is that Mckenna is so excited and passionate about this movie. She has said, “I didn't think that I would love doing fittings so much. I used to hate doing fittings.”

Because every look is so intentionally tied back to Hunger Games and she's such a big fan, it's literally like playing dress up with her. I think the fans see it, she's so relatable because she's a fan that all these fans think, "Wow, like, she's a fan and she got to do this." She’s the fangirl living out her dream, and the fans are excited for her that she finally gets to do this.

What do you think are the best kinds of projects to implement method dressing with/works best with? What does it work best with?

I think the big movies that already have a fan base, like Barbie or Wednesday, Being able to pull inspiration from existing books or films makes it so much easier for a stylist rather than a movie that no one's seen before. There's no curiosity or momentum about it because you're starting from scratch, whereas Hunger Games, Barbie, Wednesday, there's already a level of expectation.

The looks for this press run have been a mix of archival, new, and custom pieces. How do you make that choice? How important is it for you to create an archive for Mckenna?

It kind of is a mix of what we’re able to source. Mckenna really wanted to pay homage to Joanna's character with that scene where she's like, "My stylist is always putting me in trees." She's like, "I wanna do a tree reference." And I'm like, "How in the world am I gonna find a fashion reference that's a tree that's not a costume?"

I love the challenge of sourcing the market, and so do the girls on my team. I think it was 2011 Phoebe Philo where Celine did some tree references in the collection. But just because we find it online doesn't mean that we can get it. So then it's reaching out to every vintage dealer, every rental house, asking, "Do you guys have anything like this?" And they might have it, but they're like, "It's already gone, someone has it." I ended up actually finding the Celine tree dress on the RealReal, and I bought it. I love RealReal.

What is your approach to dressing different clients? For instance, you mentioned Sadie Sink earlier, can you walk me through how that process differs from Mckenna?

It's very different between each girl. I let them set the pace. If they wanna be involved, great. If they just wanna show up to the fitting and not even know what's gonna be there, I try to accommodate whatever direction they wanna go. I have one client that literally last week has sent me over 200 references of dresses that she wants, and another girl that's like, “I really don't care. Whatever you tell me to wear, I'll wear it.”

Every girl is different, and what makes my job so interesting is that it's not the same. Everyone has very different styles. I think the most important part of a job as a stylist is to keep their style true to them and not just force my style onto them. Mckenna's way more girly, Sadie is a little bit more casual, it’s just taking their style and elevating it a little bit.

Will you do any looks inspired by Mckenna’s character Maysilee? The looks have been mostly referential to things and people from past stories. Are there influences of Maysilee in the looks that fans haven't been able to pick up on because the film wasn’t out yet?

In a couple days, she’ll be in Miami for press, and she's wearing a very Maysilee inspired, purple Miu Miu dress that has a white collar. When she wears it, everyone's gonna be like, "Oh, that's Maysilee." She really wanted to have flowers and necklaces because Maysilee is really into jewelry, so it’s very light and flowery.

Can you break down the outfit for the New York City premiere?

We are doing the Mockingjay dress, the one with the wings, and that was another thing that I was very stumped on. I'm like, "What designer's gonna make these wings?" I had this woman in LA who does wings, she's done Halloween costumes and music videos.

In the first fitting, I pulled this navy Pamella Roland gown. The fabric is really, really cool. It's like a shimmery kind of organza. I thought, "That's the right color,” but I wanted it to be strapless. I went back to Pamella Roland and they were like, "We can make it in strapless." Mckenna was very keen on having some sort of embellishment to replicate Katniss because she had screen printing on the gown and it kind of looks like wings in a way.

Pamela then drew all these CADs with diamond wings on it, and then we got the wings made. We did the final fitting and I almost started to cry. Her mom's taking videos and it's epic. It's so exciting because the fans were doing polls on what she's gonna wear to the premiere.

It's full circle, we started with the wedding dress, Mckenna did the fire gown, and then we ended with the Mockingjay dress.

What was the hardest look to pull together?

I think design-wise, it was the fire gown.

Getting the fire printed on the fabric was really hard. I had a while back done a custom Cong Tri gown for Cami Mendes for the Masters of the Universe tour. It was like a gold beaded gown, and I remember I really liked the fabrics that they used for it.

So when I was thinking of who could do this fire gown, I reached out to them first, and I'm like, "Can you guys do something that looks like a fire? Like, she's literally on fire." And they're like, "No. We don't think we can." And again, they were like, "Give us some time." They came back and said, "We did all these testing on the fabric." I'm like, "Yeah, you did it. You did it."

What's really funny is we were at a fitting at Mckenna's house with the fire gown in a garment bag, and one of her friends stopped by. It was just a tip of the dress showing and her friend said, "Oh my God, you got a fire gown." Then I thought, "Okay, people are gonna get it."

#3425. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

But will the movie be any good? After all, quality has also been a problem for Marvel lately. Then again, 2026 has been considerably stronger for the Marvel Cinematic Universe on that front thanks to "Spider Man: Brand New Day" and the streaming series "Wonder Men" and "VisionQuest." So, hopefully, directors Joe and Anthony Russo will build on these successes by delivering a thrilling Avengers movie.

The merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery has resulted in the formation of Skydance, which now holds various high-profile media assets. From a news perspective, the David Ellison-led conglomerate now owns both CBS News and CNN. There’s been a considerable amount of discussion regarding the future of both entities, especially in regard to whether CBS’ Bari Weiss might run CNN. While Weiss won’t take that big seat, I’ve still been curious about a merger, and Ellison recently weighed in.

Given how internal mergers tend to happen following corporate consolidation, it is indeed reasonable to wonder whether CNN and CBS News might eventually be combined into a single entity. Ellison recently appeared at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, where he discussed various facts of the company’s overall future. In terms of the corporation’s two marquee news banners, the exec was asked if there would be “a point a year from now, two years from now, where these institutions merge.” Ellison (via Deadline) said this:

Right now, we are incredibly happy operating them basically within the status quo. I think you also have … there might be some news sharing in the future. But right now we’re operating them as they are.

So this answer pretty much seems to fall into the category of “not a definitive yes, but not a definitive no”. At the very least, the possibility of “news sharing” does make sense due to the two networks now being under the same corporate umbrella. I still can’t help but wonder, however, whether Ellison isn't totally shutting down the merger idea due to it being internally discussed as a viable option. That’s just speculation on my part, of course, but I wouldn’t be surprised if the powers that be have or are currently pondering the idea, at the very least.

Ahead of the Paramount/WB merger, there were plenty of questions regarding what it might mean for CNN. Several media pundits expressed concerns about Weiss potentially being put in charge of the Ted Turner-founded political news network. W. Kamau Bell, a former host at the network, chastised Weiss’ handling of CBS News and argued that her presence would cause an issue with editorial autonomy. Those sentiments were echoed by another former analyst, Jim Acosta, who expressed his hope that Weiss wouldn’t “murder” CNN.

Bari Weiss Addresses 60 Minutes Concerns And How She’s Handling Backlash Against CBS News

Ellison eventually confirmed this past October, however, that current CNN CEO Mark Thompson would remain in his post. Shortly thereafter, Thompson spoke about the merger and shared some complimentary thoughts on his new bosses. The CEO said that after speaking to Ellison and the other Skydance executives, he felt “real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for.” All in all, Thompson has a solid reputation, and former CBS anchor Scott Pelley also praised him while warning CNN staffers about possible editorial changes post-merger.

As Thompson continues to run CNN, Bari Weiss will remain editor-in-chief at CBS News. Interestingly enough, Weiss was recently asked if she’d be interested in running CNN at some point, and she declared she was fine with solely overseeing her current network. It’s evident that the two media outlets will remain independent for now but, if David Ellison’s recent comments are anything to go by, Weiss and Thompson may have some editorial dealings down the road.

#3422. Kate Middleton Announces Surprise Documentary About Her Cancer Journey

“Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton says, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a public event. Instead, they're the voice-over in a previously unannounced documentary about the Princess of Wales and her life since she disclosed a diagnosis of cancer in 2024.

According to Kensington Palace, which announced the film on Saturday, Heal is “a deeply personal new documentary from The Princess of Wales, exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.” It will air on the BBC in the UK on November 29, and in the US on NBCUniversal on November 30.

Heal follows Kate Middleton during her participation in one of the United Kingdom’s most demanding endurance events: The National Three Peaks Challenge, which she completed this summer. In less than 24 hours, the princess climbed the three highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales: Ben Nevis (4,413 feet), Scafell Pike (3,209 feet), and Yr Wyddfa–Snowdon (3,559 feet). The undertaking wasn't just a personal effort, as it was also in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization that supports people living with cancer before, during, and after the disease.

The documentary will also support that organization, Kensington Palace notes, saying “All funds received through the documentary's distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to help people living with and beyond cancer.” The Royal Marsden Hospital, at which Middleton received treatment, is also referenced in the film, as Middleton's brother, James, asks her “Isn’t it when you leave the Royal Marsden, you ring the bell?”

But while many patients participate in the bell-ringing ritual at the conclusion of treatment, Middleton says she missed out on that moment. “Yeah, but I didn’t ring the bell,” she replies. “So maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” James responded, suggesting her Three Peaks experience was that symbolic peal.

While Prince William is no stranger to documentary work, nor are Prince Harry and wife Meghan Markle, this is Kate Middleton's first venture into the format. Perhaps to ease her into the project, Heal's Director of Photography is a face quite familiar to the Princess: Will Warr, the filmmaker behind her video announcement marking the end of her chemotherapy treatments.

“Through this documentary, The Princess hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer and transform access to holistic cancer care which supports wellbeing, resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis,” Kensington Palace says of Heal, a message underscored by Middleton's words in the trailer. “You know, healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”

“It’s clear we're not meant to face life’s challenges alone,” the princess says as the trailer concludes. “Things can renew and grow. Often it is through pain that we realize that there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that."

#3421. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it."

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

However, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

#3420. A Doctor Doom And Doctor Strange Team-Up Is One Of The Best Marvel Comics Ever

Doctor Victor von Doom is a master of magic, so little surprise he's often crossed paths with the Sorcerer Supreme, Doctor Stephen Strange. Their first meeting, and the foundation for their mutual respect, was in 1989's "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment," one of the essential Doctor Doom comics every Marvel fan should read.

Written by Roger Stern, one of the best writers in the 1980s Marvel Comics bullpen, and drawn by Mike Mignola, future creator of the "Hellboy" universe, "Triumph and Torment" is indeed a triumph. It was published in the "Marvel Graphic Novel" line, itself designed to tell standalone and more mature stories featuring Marvel's character stable.

Doom's usual nemeses, Reed Richards and the Fantastic Four, are nowhere to be seen. While, conceptually, Doom needs Richards, tales like "Triumph and Torment" prove how he can hold individual stories without the FF. "Triumph and Torment" is also one of the most convincing arguments for Doom being more than a villain.

In Doom's debut, Stan Lee and Jack Kirby's "Fantastic Four" #5, it's established he had, during his and Reed's time at college, been obsessed with dark magic and built a machine to enter the nether world, which blew up and scarred him. His fuller origin in "Fantastic Four Annual" #2 revealed his ambition was to contact his mother, Cynthia von Doom, a witch who died during his childhood. Cynthia's trunk of magical secrets begat Victor's own knowledge of sorcery.

A 1971 story in "Astonishing Tales" #8 (by Gerry Conway and Gene Colan) then revealed that every Midsummer's Eve (when the liminal walls between worlds are the thinnest), Doom battles the forces of Hell to free his mother's soul, only to reach a stalemate. So, in "Triumph and Torment," Doom does the unthinkable and asks for help.

In "Triumph and Torment," both Strange and Doom partake in a contest of the world's greatest sorcerers held by Strange's god-like patrons, the Vishanti. Strange wins with Doom placing second — a familiar place for him, but it works in his favor. Per contest rules, Strange must grant a "boon" of Doom's choosing, and Doom wants Strange's assistance in freeing his mother's soul.

"Is one woman's soul beneath the notice of the Sorcerer Supreme?" Doom asks a surprised Strange, who in turns questions why Doom never requested his help before. "I will bear any ordeal, Strange, but Doctor Doom does not beg," he replies. That pride is ultimately crucial to Doom's plan to free Cynthia.

In Hell, facing the overwhelming power of the demon lord Mephisto, Doom seemingly trades Strange's soul for his mother's. But Cynthia, a noble woman, refuses and spurns Victor — a sacrifice that secures her place in Heaven. Doom finally frees his mother and outwits her devilish captor. This plan both flatters and damns Doom's character. He values his mother's safety more than her love for him, but his own pride most of all.

"Triumph and Torment" helps itself stand alone by exploring Doom and Strange's origins, so you can understand both men completely from this one story. Their journeys are also quite similar, as physical injuries prompt both men to venture high into the Himalayas seeking mystical knowledge. The book retells Cynthia's death, and Victor's childhood, via Doom's attendant Boris. Along with the reader, Strange realizes that beneath Doom's cold armor lies a child of tragedy. Upon taking his mask for the first time, Doom swears that pain and compassion are for lesser men — but his plan to free his mother, and what it costs him, prove otherwise.

Mike Mignola's art in "Triumph and Torment" makes Doctor Doom, his castle, and Latveria feel more truly gothic than in any other comic. Knowing Mignola went on to create a demonic superhero, too, it's hard not to compare "Triumph and Torment" to "Hellboy." Mignola drawing Strange and Doom facing down demons feels like a "Hellboy" test run in the same way his Batman comic "Sanctum" was.

In the documentary "Mike Mignola: Drawing Monsters," Mignola admitted he felt out of place drawing typical Marvel superhero books during the 1980s. "I'm not cut out to draw superheroes [...or] cars and buildings, most of the stuff that comics are made of," Mignola explained. He'd much rather be drawing monsters, which is why "Triumph and Torment" was a perfect assignment for him. Mignola's penciling especially comes to vibrant life once Doom and Strange enter Hell.

Far from looking identical, the demons all have different skin tones, weapons, and proportions. Some have wings, one is a humanoid torso on a giant serpent's tail, etc. Inker/colorist Mark Badger, rather than using a single background color for Hell, employs red-orange-yellow-green gradients. Mixed with Mignola's heavy shadows, it looks truly creepy, ethereal, and dangerous, like the typical fire and brimstone version of Hell but made even stranger. Compare this to the scary and lonely underworld in Mignola's 2010s series "Hellboy in Hell," and you can see an artist who grew.

Of course, the greatest achievement in "Triumph and Torment" is Doctor Doom's. In "Astonishing Tales" #8, Doom's goal to free his mother from eternal damnation is presented as a Sisyphean task he'll never achieve. Thinking he could break the laws of Hell is a sign of Doom's immense self-regard and ambition — and incredibly, he eventually did it.

What disappointed us was the fact that the whole storyline is revolving around us, the parents, not knowing about the pregnancy, when we already knew! We just played along.

The comment went on to state that they were under the impression the storyline was solely about Jonathan and Ally, but agreed to filming despite being uncomfortable on camera. They did ask TLC to omit the footage, but it had nothing to do with Ally's pregnancy and more their discomfort replaying that moment for television.

Now, it's always important to note that this information is still alleged, and Ally's parents could be stating this to save face after what was originally shown in 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way. Conversely, I did wonder why Jonathan and Ally would need to tell them the news when she was clearly showing.

The new information presents conflicting accounts of what happened with Jonathan and Ally, and makes me question why she was so upset afterward. If that scene was also scripted, then I'm also wondering if all the red flags that we saw were also just for the show.

90 Day Fiancé’s David Dangerfield Spoke Out After Former Fiancé Sheila Mangubat Died

This is what always happens when these conflicting stories crop up. Now I'm questioning everything that we've seen in Jonathan and Ally's storyline, and wondering what's real and what wasn't. Are the parents even telling the truth? Is anyone telling the truth?

What it sounds like is the producers wanted to recreate the scene in which Ally initially told her parents she was pregnant for the sake of the storyline. Past vets have said that's a common thing, and that it can often lead to arguments when family has to rehash past trauma.

All this to say, I'm going to be keeping a much closer eye on what's happening with Jonathan and Ally going forward. I'd also love to see if these online comments will be addressed in the tell-all special, or 90 Day Fiancé's producers will hope the drama fades before then.

Catch 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way on TLC on Sundays at 8:00 p.m. ET. This season has been very entertaining thus far, especially now that we have a great update on Armando Rubio's daughter after that scary scene.

The couple were married in the desert hot spot of Palm Springs, California on Saturday, November 21, an outdoor ceremony held at Frank Sinatra’s former mansion, with Wayne Coyne, frontman of The Flaming Lips and a Cyrus collaborator, officiating.

The 33-year-old singer and the 28-year-old musician—Morando is the drummer for the band Liily—had kept their plans a secret until Friday, when TMZ broke the news. Sinatra’s former home in Palm Springs, where the wedding took place

#3417. Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

If you're switching from Apple Music or Spotify to Tidal, you probably want to bring your playlists with you. Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz. They both have a free tier, but they only transfers a few hundred songs gratis. My playlists are way bigger than that. The easy solution is to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when your tracks are transferred, but that didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music and Spotify to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee. Here's how it works:

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection."

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

#3416. Avengers: Doomsday Trailer Finally Gives Cyclops The X-Men Line Fans Were Waiting For

If you thought the wait to finally hear Chris Evans' Steve Rogers announce (well, more like theatrically whisper), "Avengers, assemble!" in 2019's "Avengers: Endgame" was long enough, then that's nothing compared to the plight of "X-Men" enthusiasts ever since the first 20th Century Fox film came out in 2000. Arguably no fanbase has suffered more in that time, enduring a steady stream of relatively comic book-y blockbusters that mostly just seemed embarrassed of their own source material, with only a few exceptions thrown into the mix. Whatever you might say about "Avengers: Doomsday" leading up to its release, however, "comic book-y" has to be at the top of the list — and the final "Doomsday" trailer has just given us the famous line every nerd has been dying to witness.

Yes, this is a perfect excuse to link to the memorable "Say the line, Bart!" gag from "The Simpsons." "X-Men" fans have read it in the comics, they've actually seen it before in the animated "X-Men: '97" series, and it basically seemed like a fait accompli that Marvel would find a way to deliver this moment in live action for "Doomsday." You know what we're talking about: Cyclops (James Marsden), leader of the mutant team of superheroes, finally bellowing out, "To me, my X-Men!"

The only wrinkle is probably the idea of dropping this reveal in a trailer, as opposed to saving it for the movie itself. Would it have been ideal to experience this for the very first time in theaters on opening weekend, rather than on your phone while walking into work on a Monday morning? Of course! Does that make the actual scene any less thrilling? Probably not! So, without further ado, let's overanalyze this to within an inch of its life below.

Could anyone have imagined seeing this comic book panel come to life before their very eyes in "Avengers: Doomsday"? Okay, sure, the circumstances aren't exactly what most fans would've anticipated in a vacuum. Rather than seeing this moment occur after several successful "X-Men" movies spent years carefully laying the foundation for Scott Summers to become the leader of the team we know and love from the comics, this is getting shoehorned into a crossover movie pitting a few familiar "X-Men" film stars against a villain they have no real connection to in Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom. And despite the "X-Men"-centric nature of this call to action, it's at least a little funny to hear him specifically assemble his fellow mutants and then watch several members of the Avengers and Fantastic Four arrive in perfect formation.

But between the awfully long wait for this moment and James Marsden's delivery of this dialogue (which is pretty similar to the one in Season 1 of the widely well-received "X-Men '97"), it's tough to imagine many fans out there will feel inclined to nitpick anything. Directors Joe and Anthony Russo are clearly hoping this begins to set things right for a group of mutants who've deserved a much better live-action fate than they've typically received. So, while the internet spends the next few weeks arguing over whether this sequence had the requisite amount of hype and payoff to decades of build up, the rest of the moviegoing population has probably already been convinced to fork over approximately $2 billion for this latest "Avengers" extravaganza. So it goes!

The Avengers, X-Men, Fantastic Four, and more will arrive in "Avengers: Doomsday" on December 18, 2026.

#3415. Barbara Eden, 95, Breaks Down Her Fitness Routine Away From the Gym

Barbara Eden’s secret to looking and feeling great at the age of 95 involves some quality time with a personal trainer.

“I go for about, I don’t know, 35 minutes on the bike. It’s good,” Eden shared with Fox News Digital in an interview published on Sunday, November 22. “I don’t go to the gym anymore.”

When she did, the I Dream of Jeannie actress committed to a “spinning class for an hour, and then I worked with a trainer for a half hour, lifting weights.”

These days, Eden still lifts weights because she believes it’s especially good for women and their bones.

“You have to be disciplined about being active when you’re an actor,” she said with a laugh. “My husband [of 35 years, Jon Eicholtz] and I both have a trainer that comes in and helps us out.”

As any wellness expert would argue, fitness is only part of the equation to staying healthy. Diet is also important to longevity.

Eden said she is careful about what she eats, “but I’m not overly stupid about it, you know?”

“I’ve never smoked. I don’t know if that means anything. But I think one of the things that’s most important in your life is that you recognize other people,” she said. “You realize that they’re not so different than you are, and you have to get along. And when you do that, you find life is much more interesting, and people are much more interesting.”

Eden became a household name when she starred in I Dream of Jeannie from 1965 to 1970. She also guest starred in projects like Sabrina the Teenage Witch and George Lopez.

As she calls Beverly Hills home, the actress said she’s “glad I’m here, and I’m glad I’m still working.”

As she watches the younger generations grow up, Eden also wanted to share her beauty tips. While her evening routine involves washing her face and putting on moisturizer, she warns fans to watch the sun.

As she explained, Eden wished she had known “the damage the sun could do to your skin.”

“We didn’t know that when I was growing up,” she explained. “And I think it really helps, if you know, to put sunscreen, you know, on your face during the day. Or if you’re working.”

Hallmark churns out nearly a hundred new romance movies every year. The 2026 Countdown to Christmas lineup alone is slated for 34 original holiday-themed flicks. Part of the reason it’s easy for the cable channel-turned-streamer to make so many movies a year is that it has a list of dedicated actors who are eager to star in these films -- like Queen of Hallmark Lacey Chabert. And yet, somehow, they manage to keep the pairings fresh. So fresh that two of my favorite longtime Hallmark actors, Erin Cahill and Andrew Walker, just starred in their first movie together. I’m happy to report it was worth the wait!

Yep, you read that right. After spending 20 years with the cable channel and being friends for 18 years, Cahill and Walker finally got to share the screen as romantic leads in Christmas in Blue Dog Valley. The holiday flick follows Goldie MacKenzie (Cahil), a former Hollywood on-set veterinarian, who decides to leave the glitz and glamour for a slower life as the in-house veterinarian in the small town of Blue Dog Valley.

The residents of Blue Dog Valley aren’t too thrilled about an outsider taking over their beloved veterinary practice, and Goldie has to work overtime to win over the hearts of the town’s loyal pet owners. Desperate for an ally, Goldie turns to Cohen (Walker), the son of the former owner of the vet practice, for help. While they get off to a rough start, sparks start to fly as the two spend more time together, especially with Goldie taking over planning duties for the annual Christmas parade that will feature the four-legged and furry residents of the town this year.

It’s not just their characters who have love for each other, though. Both Cahill and Walker have a deep appreciation for each other and their decades-long friendship. In talking with Hallmark on set, both of these iconic stars shared how excited they were to be sharing the screen together for the first time. Take a look:

A post shared by Hallmark Channel (@hallmarkchannel)

It can be easy for the human actors to get upstaged by their animal co-stars, especially when there are so many different types of animals in a movie (cows, alpacas, and of course dogs in this case), but Cahill and Walker managed to hold things down even in the face of an adorable, overweight corgi. It’s a testament to the chemistry these two have on screen.

Their characters don’t share as much time on screen together as some of the other couples in Hallmark’s Christmas movies. However, the time they are together is swoonworthy — well, once they got over their meet-cute, that is. I definitely wouldn’t mind a sequel revisiting Goldie and Cohen a year from now. Or, better yet, I’d love to see Cahill and Walker star in even more Hallmark movies together now that it’s clear that they play compelling and entertaining romantic leads.

Blue Dog Valley might not be my favorite Hallmark Christmas movie of 2026, but it's still worth the watch. If you missed the live airing, you can stream it now with an active Hallmark+ subscription. While there, check out my favorite Cahill movie, Christmas on Cherry Lane, or my favorite Walker film, Three Wise Men and a Baby.

#3413. Cillian Murphy Regretted Not Being Part Of One Christopher Nolan Movie

Speaking to the Independent back in 2023, Cillian Murphy admitted there was one Christopher Nolan movie that he would've liked to have worked on but didn't. The film in question? Nolan's 2014 space odyssey "Interstellar."

Murphy has, to date, appeared in six of Nolan's movies. He played Dr. Jonathan Crane, aka the Scarecrow, in Nolan's three Batman movies (albeit, two of those performances were cameos), and he portrayed Robert Fischer, a man subjected to dream invasion, in "Inception." He also played a soldier in "Dunkirk" and won an Academy Award for Best Actor for portraying the titular character in Nolan's "Oppenheimer." And while he's great in all these roles, some of Murphy's performances in Nolan's films are even better than others.

As for "Interstellar," Murphy told the Independent that while he wishes he could've been involved with it, he loves it all the same, explaining:

"I adore 'Interstellar' just because I find it so emotional. [...] I remember seeing it in the cinema when I had little kids. It just had a big impact on me. It broke my heart. I love watching his films when I'm not in them because you don't have to freak out about the size of your ears, or whatever."

That said, Murphy clarified that the "right people" were ultimately cast in "Interstellar." Indeed, the film is full of big-name stars, including Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain, John Lithgow, Michael Caine, Ellen Burstyn, Casey Affleck, Topher Grace, David Oyelowo, and Matt Damon. Given the prestige of that cast, Murphy likely would've been happy to tag in for any of those actors.

Cillian Murphy was interviewed by the Independent right around the time "Oppenheimer" opened in theaters, and it was brought to his attention that many filmgoers had, amusingly, paired the movie with Greta Gerwig's "Barbie" to create a deliberately incongruous double-feature widely referred to as "Barbenheimer." It was quite the cultural event as well, with "Barbenheimer" going on to become a massive box office success.

Playfully, the Independent asked Murphy which Christopher Nolan film he would pair "Oppenheimer" with, and he presented the following options:

"You could go 'Interstellar,' which is very ... explores similar scientific, physic themes. Or you could watch 'Dunkirk,' which is also set in World War II. 'Dunkirk' is shorter, so that might be a good match 'cause it's like an hour-and-a-half, and then you can go into ['Oppenheimer']."

"Dunkirk" is, just for the record, 106 minutes, but I get Murphy's meaning. "Oppenheimer" is already three hours, and "Interstellar" is 169 minutes, so pairing two very long movies together might be a bit of a chore.

Nolan has since directed the 2026 mega-hit "The Odyssey," while, in the same year, Murphy made his long-awaited return to the "28" franchise by appearing briefly in "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple." One can assume, however, that Murphy and Nolan will cross paths again professionally in due time.
