#3365. 10 Saddest Deaths in 'Sunrise on the Reaping,' Ranked

Spoiler Alert: This list contains spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.The Hunger Games has never been shy about putting its characters through absolute misery, and Sunrise on the Reaping is no exception. Set during the 50th year of the Games—its Second Quarter Quell—the latest chapter in Suzanne Collins' dystopian saga follows a young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) as he's thrown into an arena designed to be twice as deadly as the usual Games, with 48 tributes fighting for survival.

But as brutal as the competition itself is, it's the people Haymitch loses along the way that make this story truly one of the most devastating additions to the franchise. From friendships forged in the arena to the loved ones left behind in District 12, Sunrise on the Reaping is filled with so many deaths that have left a mark on the young tribute as well as audiences alike. So, here are some of the most poignant ones.

Panache Barker (Jhaleil Swaby) is one of the District 1 Career tributes who enters the Quarter Quell with a clear advantage over many of the other participants. Having already trained since young, he quickly established himself as a dangerous threat, with his arrogance, brute strength, and aggression already creating conflict before the games even began. But Panache's confidence ultimately proves to be his downfall in the arena, as Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace) uses her poisoned darts to stealthily kill him, right as he's about to deliver a fatal attack on Haymitch.

Having built himself up as the ruthless antagonist of the games, Panache's sudden takedown isn't particularly heartbreaking on its own. In fact, it initially feels like a moment of relief and dark irony, since he was, after all, constantly brutalizing the other tributes—and seemingly enjoying it. However, despite his actions, there remains an underlying tragedy as Panache is simply just another teenager who was manipulated by the Capitol into becoming a cruel killer. A mere cog in the endless machine.

As another District 1 Career, Silka Sharp (Laura Marcus) was undoubtedly ruthless and skilled—so much so that she became one of the last tributes standing in the arena alongside Haymitch. Their final confrontation is a tense battle that leaves Haymitch badly wounded, and Silka seemingly having the upper hand. But when she corners him towards the area's edge, Haymitch uses the hidden force field to his advantage, taunting her to throw her axe and have the weapon rebound to fatally strike her.

Similar to Panache, Silka's death isn't necessarily upsetting, as it's staged as a pure, triumphant "outsmarting the villain" climax. That's what happens when she's consistently positioned as a lethal powerhouse who's actively gunning to spill blood and win. But she, too, is a tragic product of the Capitol's cruel system. Unfortunately, the movie omits an important book moment of vulnerability that showcased this (yes, we're talking about the chocolate scene).

Wellie (Rada Rae) is one of the Newcomers from District 6, and as one of the youngest competitors in the arena, it's understandable why Haymitch was quick to care for her before the games began. We see this as he offers Wellie his lunch during one of the tribute's meal sessions. Unfortunately, we don't get much from her after that, as her death occurs off-screen with Haymitch finding her body after Silka rings Wellie's bicycle bell as a means to lure him into an ambush.

While the discovery is obviously grim and heartbreaking, audiences who haven't read the book have very little time to get attached to Wellie before she dies. In fact, the film effectively glosses over the important bond forged between Haymitch and Wellie in the game. They even soften her actual death—which was arguably the most gruesome and brutal one of all. Nevertheless, her death still remains an emotional gut punch as she symbolizes the tragic loss of innocents.

Entering the Second Quarter Quell alongside his other District 12 tributes, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang) quickly becomes a sympathetic figure. Despite the initial hostility surrounding his family's role as oddsmakers—people who took bets on the Hunger Games—Wyatt earns the trust of his fellow tributes and proves that he's willing to protect those who are more vulnerable than himself. Of course, we see this right at the start of the games, during the chaotic Cornucopia bloodbath, as he steps in front of Silka's axe-throw to shield young Lou Lou (Iona Bell).

In this case, his death is truly upsetting because it comes from an act of kindness and sacrifice rather than selfishness or ambition. Wyatt isn't trying to win at someone else's expense. He simply wants to protect Lou Lou, a girl who has already been subjected to the Capitol's cruel manipulation. His willingness to put himself in harm's way makes him an easy character to root for, and his death only reinforces how little room the Games leave for such compassion.

Lou Lou is a tragic figure from the moment she is introduced, as she's essentially sent in as a mere body-double since the Capitol had to cover up the accidental death of Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). Seemingly drugged (or at least conditioned) into playing a role she doesn't fully understand, the girl is thrust into the Games without any control over her own circumstances. Despite surviving the initial bloodbath, she meets her end when she inhales poisonous pollen from the deadly plants scattered throughout the arena.

Naturally, what makes Lou Lou's death so tragic is the sheer indignity of her existence in the Games. For one, her fate was immediately set as she was sent in as a sacrificial pawn—one who doesn't even get to die under her real name. The books at least give hints about her past, but they also reinforce the disturbing lengths the Capitol is willing to go to in order to maintain the illusion of its spectacle. Lou Lou is one of the many victims of a system that sees children as disposable, and her fate is a reminder that the cruelty of the Games extends far beyond the arena's physical dangers.

The tragedy of Louella McCoy is how her death happens before she even gets the chance to enter the arena. During the tribute parade, the horses pulling the chariots are spooked by objects thrown onto the track, causing them to panic and crash. Haymitch is thrown off, while Louella is sadly left trapped in the District 12 chariot, which flips over and drags her across the path. It's brutal to watch and utterly shocking, especially since it sets the stage for Haymitch to boil with anger and openly defy President Snow (Ralph Fiennes).

Incredibly young and never even given the opportunity to fight for her own life, Louella is killed by the very spectacle that the Capitol insists is meant to honor them. If anything, it exposes just how careless and cruel the system (and its people) truly are, particularly since they flippantly replace her with another girl the next day. By erasing her loss, the Capitol once again strips a child of their dignity, just for the sake of maintaining the illusion of control.

Despite her sharp-tongued nature, Maysilee Donner grows to become one of Haymitch's closest allies as they fight to protect each other across the area. But as the number of tributes begins to dwindle, the two consciously decide to go their separate ways as neither wants to watch the other die (or be responsible for it). Moments later, a cannon fires, and they rush back towards each other, only for a flock of bird mutts to fatally attack Maysilee, with Haymitch scrambling to protect her in his arms.

Of course, the moment is agonizing to watch as Maysilee isn't just another tribute Haymitch loses along the way. She's a slice of home and a true friend who shares his determination to survive without surrendering completely to the brutality of the Capitol. Yes, there are significant changes from the book that shape her death as collateral punishment for Haymitch rather than a direct consequence of her own acts of rebellion. However, the stellar performance between Zada and Grace makes up for this omission, with their chemistry carrying the emotional weight of a relationship built on genuine care and humanity—even as they're in a competition designed to strip its participants of precisely that.

As the son of the legendary victor, Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV) is a clever and resourceful young boy who helps recruit Haymitch to sabotage the Games as a means to undermine the Capitol's control. Their plan succeeds in disrupting the system, but the Capitol retaliates by unleashing vicious squirrel mutts on Ampert. Haymitch finds him being attacked and desperately tries to intervene. Sadly, the creatures horrifically overwhelm the young tribute, leaving Haymitch unable to save him.

Ampert's death is particularly tragic because he symbolizes the devastating risks of daring to challenge an authoritarian regime. Like some others, the young boy's fate of death was already sealed thanks to his father's prior acts of rebellion. As a result, his courage and willingness to risk everything for a chance at freedom only makes his loss all the more shattering—especially since it happens in such a brutal manner (one that's even worse and more gruesome in the books).

After unexpectedly surviving the Second Quarter Quell and returning to District 12 as a victor, Haymitch is confronted with the consequences of his defiance: his home is engulfed in flames where both his mother (Kara Tointon) and little brother, Sid (Smylie Bradwell), were trapped inside. Of course, it's clear that President Snow has made good on his threats, with Haymitch having nothing to do but watch as his entire family is taken from him. To make matters worse, the tragedy becomes even more painful when they reveal that mother and son were found holding onto each other, resulting in them being buried in the same casket.

There's something especially cruel about this punishment, as Haymitch's family are true innocents. Neither knew of his plans, and yet they were forced to pay the price. In this sense, Snow isn't merely trying to silence a rebellious victor. He's making an example of Haymitch and ensuring that his victory comes with a lifetime of suffering. The loss of Ma and Sid also strips Haymitch of the very support system he desperately needs after the Games, leaving him isolated and increasingly broken. It's a deeply personal act of vengeance, and one that helps explain why Haymitch eventually retreats into deep despair.

Just when you think Haymitch has lost so much, he's met with another devastating blow. After the funeral of his family and fellow tributes, he finally reunites with his long-love, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), who has finally been released from captivity. And for a fleeting moment, their reunion offers a glimmer of hope as she happily pulls out a bag of gumdrops she found on the rocks, thinking them to be a gift. Haymitch, in turn, feeds one to her—only for him to quickly realize that it was a trap planted by Snow. Once again, he's left helpless in his desperation and can do nothing but watch someone he loves die in his arms.

Her death is distressing not just because it's Lenore Dove, but because of what she represents to Haymitch. Throughout the film, she's one of the few people who genuinely understands his anger at the Capitol and even encourages him to believe things can change. She isn't simply a romantic interest, but a person whose conviction and rebellious spirit help shape the person Haymitch becomes. Even as she dies, Lenore Dove makes him promise to keep fighting against the oppressive system, turning her final moments into one last act of defiance. And knowing what Haymitch's emotional journey looks like in the future makes this loss all the more heartbreaking as audiences realize that it's his memories of the people he loved that have kept him going.

Percy Jackson & The Olympians is one of the most popular Greek mythology book series since the turn of the century, which is saying something because our fascination with the old stories has never completely ceased. The stories continue to be reimagined, whether on the screen or in books, every day. However, there’s something unique and special about the Percy Jackson books. Luckily, it’s a great time to be a fan.

Rick Riordan continues to expand the Riordanverse, which includes Percy Jackson and other mythological series like the Kane Chronicles, all the time. Plus, the story is back on the TV screen. Disney+’s Percy Jackson season 3 has received overwhelmingly positive reviews, with special praise for its fight sequences and its darker tone.

What’s more, publishers have noticed Percy Jackson's popularity over the past two decades, and they’ve catered to fans of this series and general Greek mythology lovers. Plenty of books exist that are perfect for Percy Jackson fans who read them when they were younger and are now adults. These seventeen stand out for their spirit of adventure, their imagination, and their ability to capture Greek myths in new ways.

One of the most thrilling parts of the Percy Jackson books is that they put Greek mythology and characters into our world, rather than taking the reader back to their world. These modern books function on the same principle, imagining how the Greek gods and their children would fare if they existed nowadays. Lightning & Thunder, which I’ve had the chance to read ahead of its release, has a more optimistic view of that prospect, while Gods Behaving Badly has a darkly comedic view of the gods struggling. Either way, though, it's extremely entertaining.

Stone Blind by Natalie Haynes, Andromeda by E.S. McLeod, Clytemnestra by Costanza Casati, Circe by Madeline Miller, I, Medusa by Ayana Gray

Many of the best retellings of Greek myths center on overlooked, villainized characters, matching Percy Jackson’s core values. The series has always been about outsiders, and Rick Riordan amplifies voices of characters typically silenced. What’s more, he encourages empathy for characters like Luke, who could easily be dismissed as villains. These five are standout choices.

The Games Gods Play by Abigail Owen, Blood of Hercules by Jasmine Mas, ODY-C by Matt Fraction & Christian Ward, Arch-Conspirator by Veronica Roth

Some of the most thrilling examples of Greek mythology books place the gods and heroes in an entirely new fantasy or science fiction setting. It’s a fun thought experiment. How would these characters we know and love fare in a different world. This leads to entertaining high-stakes stories like The Games Gods Play and Blood of Hercules, where the characters are underdogs trying to survive. Meanwhile, ODY-C and Arch-Conspirator not only reimagines the gods but also the technology of the world. Luckily, they all share the same spirit of adventure as Percy Jackson, but with adult maturity.

Now is the perfect time to dive into The Games Gods Play and the rest of Abigail Owen's The Crucible series because the third book in the series, The Wrath Gods Reap, came out just this month, and it is the best book of the series. It's faster-paced, higher-stakes, and it finally gives readers an emotional payoff that's 3 books in the making.

A Thousand Ships by Natalie Haynes, The Song of Achilles by Madeline Miller, The End Crowns All by Bea Fitzgerald, Troy: Lord of the Silver Bow by David Gemmell

The Iliad and The Odyssey are probably the most popular Greek myths in existence, continually being brought to the screen or the page in new ways. Even Percy Jackson had its own take on the latter epic poem with Sea of Monsters. These four books offer new perspectives and fun adventures that will be perfect for folks who want more adventure and tension.

#3360. Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change

In “Gaslit,” a new documentary about climate change activists, Jane Fonda stands outside one of Formosa Petrochemical’s Texas facilities and looks through a thermal camera. The Oscar-winning actress is brought to tears by what she sees: a tremendous expulsion of methane gas into the air.

“Methane is 80 percent more destructive to the climate, in terms of global warming, than carbon dioxide,” Fonda explained during a recent Zoom interview. “It’s the most destructive chemical that we’re using, and it’s extremely dangerous for people. And yet here it is billowing into the air, and nobody even knows it.”

For years, Fonda has been sounding the alarm about the looming environmental catastrophe that will take place if the world doesn’t wean itself off fossil fuels. She launched a series of climate change protests dubbed “Fire Drill Fridays” in 2019 — a reference to activist Greta Thunberg’s charge that people should “act as if your house is on fire” — and has been arrested multiple times for civil disobedience. Fonda is embracing the cause with the same passion that has led her to speak out on everything from the Vietnam War to feminism to LGBTQ+ rights. But she worries her efforts may not be enough. Related Stories Paul Thomas Anderson’s ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Getting Nationwide Release in January Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’

“Our emission of global warming chemicals has gone way up since Donald Trump has become president,” Fonda said. “And of course the concern is always: Have we passed too many tipping points or a tipping point? Many climate scientists say if we act fast now, it won’t be too late. But it’s very hard to act fast when Trump is president.”

The political winds are changing. The midterms were a blue wave election that saw Democrats take back the House and the Senate in commanding fashion. They not only performed well in liberal bastions, but also captured the governor’s mansion in Texas and elected James Talarico to a U.S. Senate seat that has been in Republican hands for decades. Much of “Gaslit” focuses on the environmental damage wrought by the oil fields in West Texas’ Permian Basin. Will the change in leadership make a difference?

“It won’t hurt,” Fonda said. “I don’t know how strong Talarico is on these issues. We can’t do too much until our members are seated, and we actually have the majority in the House in January.”

“Renewables are ready,” she added. “They’re cheap. They’re safe. They’re job-intensive. It’s the perfect solution. It’s right there. It makes all the sense in the world. The only thing we lack is political will, and hopefully, with this swath of new people that have been elected to the House and the Senate, we will have the political will when we take power to turn this around.”

Fonda believes average citizens concerned about climate change can’t afford to be passive.

“One of the most important things that people can do is to demand that their elected officials pass legislation that makes these polluters pay for what they’re doing,” Fonda said. “Right now, it’s consumers, it’s us taxpayers that have to pay for the damage. They should pay, and we have to stop the $21 billion annual subsidies that we pay them. They make trillions of dollars of profit. If we cancel those subsidies, it would spell the beginning of the end for fossil fuels.”

Fonda is blunt in her warnings that the chaos and damage that global warming has caused will only accelerate unless the world switches to renewable sources of energy. Her assessment is sober, even terrifying, but one thing that gives her hope is the work that the activists highlighted in “Gaslit” are doing. “Gaslit” was financed and produced by the environmental group Greenpeace USA, and it focuses on people in the Gulf Coast and Texas who are trying to change things across the political spectrum. They range from a Republican cattle rancher, who has seen what the oil and gas business has done to his family’s land, to cancer survivors and community organizers who are hoping to change hearts and minds about fossil fuels.

“What is so moving to me about the film is we’re showing these people who do not give up; they will not,” Fonda said. “All of these activists are so brave and so incredible. They inspire me.”

“Gaslit” was directed by Katie Camosy. It is now available to rent or buy on Amazon Prime and Documentary+. As of November 19, the film can be streamed on the Greenpeace USA YouTube channel, with additional platforms rolling out.

#3359. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

On the other hand, it took 16 years for the combined power of Universal and Paramount (a Skydance Company) to will another “Focker” movie into existence, during which time someone realized that it might be kinda funny if Robert De Niro said the words “Jamba Juice.”

And in fairness, they weren’t wrong. A Robert De Niro character shouldn’t know what Jamba Juice is, let alone want to drink there! Not only that, but he correctly emphasizes the “JAM” of it all, the formal precision of which suggests that Jack — a red-blooded Boomer who’s recently become an exercise-obsessed vegan health nut — has developed a sincere degree of respect for the smoothie chain and its various blended offerings, even if it’s taken him 16 years to do so.

Given that John Hamburg’s “Focker In-Law” brings back so much of the franchise’s original cast almost three decades since they first played these roles, the film benefits from a Linklater-esque sense of temporal continuity that invites us to imagine the time between movies as a living space. Don’t be fooled by the gruel-thin story, the parade of self-amused callbacks, or the painfully contrived jokes that substitute for real emotion, this isn’t an opportunistic cash-grab meant to capitalize on our collective appetite for big screen comedies — it’s a family reunion.

the expectations for a legacy sequel are much lower than they might be for the most expensive video game in history, especially in the context of a franchise that’s sustained by the idea that the surname “Focker” sounds almost indistinguishable from the word “fucker.” (Don’t be embarrassed if you hadn’t put that together before — it’s subtle, and film critics are professionally trained to identify such things). “GTA VI” had to revolutionize interactive entertainment in order to be considered a success. “Focker In-Law” just has to deliver more of the same. It does that over and over and over again; I don’t know about Jack’s nipples, but Greg (Ben Stiller) can certainly milk an old joke until it turns to dust in his hand.

The cinematic equivalent of half-rotten Thanksgiving leftovers that you’d only eat in lieu of having any other food in the house, “Focker In-Law” might be an increasingly rare big-screen comedy, but it’s endowed with the “whatever”-level apathy of the worst straight-to-streaming junk. Depressingly, that feels like a systemic failure more than a creative one, as Hamburg is a very funny guy who directed several of the better comedies of this century’s pre-Netflix era (e.g. “Along Came Polly”), and he’s far from the only proven talent who gets wasted here.

The basic story — for which Hamburg shares credit with Austen Earl and, curiously, Ilana Glazer — offers a natural riff on the franchise’s initial premise: Greg might wear Radiohead t-shirts and sport facial skin tighter than any scene in the movie around him, but he’s now older than Jack was during the first movie, which means he and his wife Pam (Teri Polo, making the easiest money of her life) have aged into the “Parents” who are due to be “Meet”-ed when their son Henry (an overqualified Skyler Gisondo) brings his big-eyed new girlfriend Olivia (Ariana Grande) to Jack’s 80th birthday celebration.

The joke, and it’s not a bad one, is that Greg — a beta male bozo who’s desperate to make his children and their partners feel welcome — immediately bumps against his probable daughter-in-law, while Jack — a dominant and unyielding patriarch whose “Circle of Trust” is harder to crack than a captured enemy spy — cottons to her from the moment she gets to his house. It helps, of course, that Olivia is an ultra-rigid life coach and former hostage negotiator who shares Jack’s taste for military discipline, as well as his knowledge of different polygraph technologies. Why she’s drawn to a softboi like Greg’s son remains unclear, but the “Wicked”-like theatricality of Grande’s performance is farcical enough for such open questions to be their own reward (it makes sense that her character would be so emotive and intentional), and at the end of the day what matters is just that Greg has a reason to feel rejected all over again.

He doesn’t take it well! In fact, he acts like a massive asshole about it to a degree that steers the movie away from cringe comedy comfort food and closer towards a character study about a malignant narcissist instead. Stiller is a maestro of self-involved unpleasantness (his work in “Greenberg” and “The Meyerowitz Stories” has never gotten the recognition it deserves), but that kind of toxicity is far more unpleasant in the context of a film that thinks it’s cute and/or easily redeemable.

In “Meet the Parents,” Greg got into all sorts of wacky trouble because he meant well and cared so much about seeming worthy of Jack’s daughter. In “Focker In-Law,” the hijinks stem from the fact that he’s a scheming monster who’s trying to sabotage his son’s relationship so that Henry might stay closer to home. The clean and simple fun of watching good intentions curdle into misunderstood chaos has been replaced by the dull ache of watching someone try to pass off diagnosable psychosis as the stuff of routine parental anxiety.

Alarm bells start ringing from the very first comic setpiece, in which a classic setup — Greg tries to cut the airplane bathroom line by sneaking from coach into first class — is almost completely undone by the logic gaps that have come to define the character. Why does he impulsively steal Olivia’s birth control out of her bag before he even knows who she is, and how is it possible that such an overbearing dad hasn’t even seen a picture of his son’s very serious new girlfriend? Such questions aren’t really worth answering, and Hamburg at least has the courtesy to distract us from them with a fly-by cameo by Cole Escola, but the vibe is all the way off by the time we even touch down in New Jersey for the main event, and nothing that happens there is remotely inspired enough to redeem the pervasive sense that no one can remember why “Meet the Parents” became a franchise in the first place.

Was it Owen Wilson’s amusingly oblivious performance as Pam’s charmed ex-fiancé, Kevin? There’s only one way to find out! Was it Jack’s penchant for lie-detector tests or his affinity for unlovable pets? Let’s give them both a shot and see what sticks. (I was amused by the German shepherd he trains in this film, who sets up a very good joke accusation that I don’t want to spoil here). Maybe it became a phenomenon because people crave manic setpieces that end in a plume of human ashes — we should run that back just in case. Anything to avoid the obvious and enduring coziness of a “home for the holidays” movie, which “Focker In-Law” inexplicably forfeits by setting its story at the height of summer.

The ballad of Gaylord Focker certainly didn’t become a thing because of Greg’s daughter and her long-term boyfriend, whose presence this movie struggles to accommodate despite the fact that Beanie Feldstein and Eduardo Franco are both eager to help liven things up. In fairness, why open the floor to potentially amusing new characters when you can spend half the film’s runtime agonizing over Greg’s uncomfortably demented attempts to steal the engagement ring that Henry wants to give to Olivia? Some opportunities are just too good to pass up, I suppose.

That “Focker In-Law” maintains any of its series’ long-faded charm can be attributed to De Niro, who sleepwalked through the previous two sequels but feels revived by Jack’s newfound looseness in this one. The actor delights in playing off Grande’s type-A eagerness, just as his character takes a muted pleasure in how much Olivia causes Greg to crash out. In a comedy as flat, stilted, and generic as this one, De Niro’s still-inimitable star power is almost enough to save the movie from its own reheated cynicism. “JAM-ba Juice.” They actually just go by “Jamba” now. The franchise’s juice is long, long gone.

Universal Pictures will release “Focker In-Law” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3356. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3355. Steam Officially Launches Its 2026 Game of the Year Awards Voting

The Golden Joysticks has already weighed in on 2026's Game of the Year and The Game Awards has revealed its nominees for this year's best of the best. But one awards ceremony stands apart from the typical Game of the Year awards contest: the Steam Awards.

On Monday, Valve opened up nominations for its fan-voted awards, which include Game of the Year and what promises to be a highly contested category: the Hall of Fame Award. That brand-new category will pit a list of winners of the Steam Awards’ Game of the Year category from the past 10 years against each other to celebrate a decade of Valve's awards.

From now until Monday, Nov. 30 at 10 a.m. PST, Steam users can vote on the following categories, in addition to the Hall of Fame Award.

The final nominees will be revealed, and voting for the 2026 Steam Awards will begin, on Thursday, Dec. 17. That same day, the Steam Winter Sale kicks off. That's one week to the day after The Game Awards 2026, meaning that if any PC game was slighted by that awards ceremony, Steam users will have a chance to rebuke the TGAs voting body. (One thing that Steam Awards voters won't get to weigh in on is this year's GOTY frontrunner, Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar Games hasn't announced a PC version of the game yet.)

Last year's Steam Awards Game of the Year was Hollow Knight: Silksong. Other big winners from last year's Steam Awards include Baldur’s Gate 3, Hades 2, Peak, Silent Hill f, Arc Raiders, and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.

#3354. Everything We Know About Spider-Man & Wolverine Being In Avengers: Doomsday

It's almost time for Avengers: Doomsday, and rumors swirl that Spider-Man and Wolverine will turn up. Marvel is determined to one-up even Avengers: Endgame, with this movie bringing back heroes from the last 26 years of Marvel blockbusters. The final Doomsday trailer divides its time between Steve Rogers and the X-Men, and even marked a franchise first: we finally got James Marsden's Cyclops saying an iconic line, "To me, my X-Men."

The X-Men, the Fantastic Four, and several different teams of Avengers are all going up against Robert Downey, Jr.'s Doctor Doom. But with the entire multiverse expected to end ahead of next year's Avengers: Secret Wars, we're all pretty certain there are going to be a lot more surprises. There have been particularly exciting rumors about both Spider-Man and Wolverine, but how likely are they to be true?

There's currently no evidence Tom Holland's Spider-Man is in Avengers: Doomsday. The core issue lies in the real-world, with the fact there are only small gaps in Holland's schedule where he could have been available for filming; he was occupied on The Odyssey through most of Doomsday's production, before moving on to Spider-Man: Brand New Day. If he does make an appearance at all, it would have to be a very small one indeed.

That said, there's intense debate about whether the end of Spider-Man: Brand New Day is actually Doomsday setup. It shows Ned Leeds' "Spider-Tracker" app losing Spider-Man completely, only to spot him in space. This is most likely a multiversal collision known as an incursion, where two different Earths collide. It's possible Holland's Spider-Man has been transported to another Earth, one that's about to impact Earth-616.

Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield both reprised their roles in Spider-Man: No Way Home, meaning they've already been part of the Multiverse Saga. It wouldn't be at all surprising to see them turn up; in fact, there have been rumors Doomsday kicks off with Maguire's Spider-Man killed in battle with the X-Men, who are fighting to save their universe. We'll have to wait and see whether that actually happens.

One thing's for sure: If Maguire or Garfield do return as Spider-Man in Avengers: Doomsday, it's likely to only be for a small role. The film principally involves three different Earths: Earth-616, the Fantastic Four's world, and the X-Men's. That already means Doomsday has a lot of cast to juggle (even more, given Doctor Doom may have been collecting people from other timelines as well). Many characters are likely to be relegated to cameos, just to make the story navigable.

Marvel is keeping very quiet about whether Hugh Jackman's Wolverine is in Doomsday. That said, the House of Ideas do seem intent on keeping Jackman on board till he's 90 (at least), and Deadpool and Wolverine brought the character into the Multiverse Saga. In this case, it feels likely Wolverine is being kept back as a surprise. But nobody will be shocked should Logan pop his claws and fight alongside the rest of the X-Men. Perhaps he's even one of the heroes who responds to Cyclops' call to arms in the trailer.

Speaking as a lifelong X-Men fan, I'm delighted to see other members of the team get the spotlight in Doomsday's marketing. Fox depended far too much on Wolverine's popularity, and it's been so good to see Marvel course-correct a little, choosing to emphasize the likes of Professor X and Cyclops. I'm sure there are going to be more X-Men surprises, too.

Oddly enough, though, there are actually quite a few heroes couldn't missing from Avengers: Doomsday's roll call. Sticking with the X-Men, two characters stand out: Ryan Reynold's Deadpool and Famke Janssen's Jean Grey. The former has already appeared in the Multiverse Saga, and even has connections to the Time Variance Authority. The latter is an absolute powerhouse (literally the Phoenix), so there's likely a story reason here. Perhaps Jean has already been killed (or recruited) by Doctor Doom.

Far too many heroes from Earth-616 are still absent. Brie Larson's Captain Marvel is surprising, again because she's one of the most powerful heroes in play. A multiversal event really should feature the "boss of space," so we can only hope she's going to turn up. Teyonah Parris' Spectrum was stranded in the X-Men timeline at the end of The Marvels, which should surely mean she's unwittingly triggering an incursion between Earth-616 and the X-Men universe. It would actually be rather odd for Marvel to ignore her in Doomsday.

The problem, of course, is that the MCU expanded a little too quickly during the Multiverse Saga. We were introduced to so many different superheroes; some are street level (such as Alaqua Cox's Echo), while others didn't prove especially popular (the less said about Secret Invasion's new Super-Skrulls, the better). Avengers: Doomsday already faces a huge challenge if it's to give due time to multiple Avengers teams as well as the X-Men, so some Earth-616 heroes are going to be neglected. Don't expect to see the Eternals anytime soon.

That said, Marvel did recently confirm two new heroes for Doomsday. Hailee Steinfeld is returning as Kate Bishop, meaning at least one of Marvel's two Hawkeyes (and, in this case, a Young Avenger in the comics) is due to appear. Meanwhile, VisionQuest's post-credits scene confirmed Doctor Doom has resurrected Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch, presumably confirming rumors Wanda Maximoff is one of the Latverian Witches we see in the recent trailer. If these two heroes are also back, then it's possible Marvel has quite a few surprises in the works. We'll find out more when Avengers: Doomsday finally releases in December.

#3353. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money. It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. #3352. Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script

Steven Spielberg has directed musicals, sci-fi epics, adventure films, and biopics, but one genre has eluded him over the course of his decades-long career. He has never directed a Western, despite having openly longed to put his spin on the type of movies that turned one of his idols, John Ford, into a legend.

Well, the wait is over. Spielberg is developing an untitled film for Focus Features about two fugitives charting a course across the American West, and he’s assembled a crack team to help him. The ensemble will include Jessie Buckley, fresh off her Oscar win for “Hamnet,” Cillian Murphy, the Oscar-winning star of “Oppenheimer,” and Mark Rylance, a frequent Spielberg collaborator who won, you guessed it, an Oscar for “Bridge of Spies.” Related Stories ‘Focker In-Law’ Review: An Eager Ariana Grande Isn’t Enough to Save a Comedy Sequel That Can’t Remember What People Liked About This Franchise Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change

But there’s more to get cinephiles’ hearts racing! Paul Thomas Anderson, the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind “Boogie Nights,” “There Will Be Blood,” and “One Battle After Another,” is writing the script. It’s based on Kevin Barry’s novel, “The Heart in Winter.” Though Anderson usually directs his screenplays, he’s done script doctoring for Ridley Scott (“Napoleon”) and Martin Scorsese (“Killers of the Flower Moon” and the upcoming “What Happens at Night”). He also did some work on “Corky Romano” — hey, they can’t all be winners! So why not join Spielberg’s merry band?

Spielberg is still one of the all-time greats, but he could use a hit. “Disclosure Day,” which marked his return to summer movies, was a box office disappointment, and his most recent films, like “The Fabelmans” and “West Side Story,” struggled to connect with audiences despite earning excellent reviews. Maybe saddling up will be just what the movie gods ordered.

Kristie Macosko Krieger, Sara Murphy, Anderson, and Spielberg will produce the film, which is expected to hit theaters in 2028. Tim Headington, Neil Shah, Ryan Zacarias, and Ana Leocha will executive produce it.

#3351. The 5 Most Unwatchable James Bond Movies, Ranked

The James Bond franchise has long stood as one of cinema’s most defining blockbuster titles. From the outset, way back when it started with Sean Connery in the lead role in 1962’s Dr. No, it has epitomized the suave spectacle and sophisticated charm of high-octane spy thrills. Ranging from Goldfinger to Skyfall, the saga has delivered some of the most exhilarating spy-action movies ever made, but any franchise that features 25 movies is bound to have a few misfires and, unfortunately, 007 is no different.

When the franchise is at its worst, it reduces its tropes to being crude caricatures of the genre. The gadgets become goofy, the Bond girl an affront to any form of progressive femininity, and the story often suffers most under the strain of forced stylistic choices, laughably cartoonish action sequences, and a sense of antagonism that is utterly ridiculous. Ranging from early errs that were painfully anachronistic even when they were released to more modern missteps, these blundering Bond movies represent cinema’s greatest franchise at its unwatchable worst.

Released 12 years after Connery's last Bond outing—1971’s Diamonds Are Forever—and marking just the second and latest non-Eon-produced Bond movie ever made, Never Say Never Again emerged amid a time of chaos and calamity for the franchise. Roger Moore’s ongoing tenure as the official 007 had begun to falter, and while his worst movies mark some of the franchise’s lowest points, they are made watchable through a sense of characterful campiness and, in some cases, a certain so-bad-it’s-good appeal. Neither of those attributes can be applied to Never Say Never Again, which sees a 53-year-old Connery return to the role to deliver what is effectively a tame rehash of Thunderball.

The lack of originality in the picture is only worsened by the fundamental Bond staples it was deprived of. Given it wasn’t an Eon Productions project, it never had access to the iconic Bond theme, the opening gun-barrel shot, or John Barry’s signature score. Without these qualities, the film lands with a certain flatness. It lacks authentic action-thriller energy, and its efforts to at least modernize the character by implementing ‘80s trends like arcade-style dueling only make it all the more outdated today. It isn’t the worst or most egregious Bond movie ever made, but it is among the most banal, and that pervasive sense of muted mediocrity makes it an unwatchable snoozefest in 2026.

Quantum of Solace is as bland and banal a Bond movie as has ever been made. The follow-up to Daniel Craig’s dashing debut in Casino Royale undoubtedly fell victim to the 2007/08 writer’s strike in Hollywood, making it indistinguishable from any run-of-the-mill, B-grade spy thriller. It lacks the ruthless hard-edged grunt of its predecessor, the snappy stylistic flourishes of its successor, and refuses to implement anything in the way of camp charm or thematic prowess. Even the villain’s environmental slant is ill-explored, making him an odd and forgettable concoction of timely ideals and traditional egomaniacal Bond villainy.

It is ultimately a Bond movie that lacks an identity. It doesn’t strive to be anything unique, refusing to stretch beyond the safe limitations of the franchise at its most middling and mediocre. To say it is an outright terrible film would perhaps be going too far, it just stands as a flick that has no aspiration of what it wants to be. Again, the writer’s strike of the time was definitely a limiting factor on what Quantum of Solace could achieve, but for a Bond movie to be plain boring is unforgivable. Even many of the worst installments of the franchise have their goofy eccentricities that at least give them something, but Quantum of Solace lacks anything memorable, and it derides viewers of any reason to want to rewatch it.

Most, if not all, of the original Connery Bond films have elements that haven’t aged all too well. In the best of them, it’s easily dismissed as a sign of the times, but in the lesser entries of his tenure as 007, it’s a bit more grating to watch. His fifth outing, You Only Live Twice, is the epitome of this notion. It lacks the pizzazz and pop of Connery’s earlier, more iconic movies, and it seems as though Connery himself knows it more than anyone. His performance is uncharacteristically wooden, a stilted cutout of a character where his charisma and quick-wit ought to be.

Bereft of Connery’s best work, the film struggles to apply wallpaper over the narrative cracks and biting insensitivities. Roald Dahl’s screenplay leans heavily on racial stereotypes—an idea that reaches an ugly crescendo with Bond’s infamous “yellowface” disguise as a Japanese man—and his endeavor to up the ante comes at an emotional cost. The movie is a big, drab blockbuster with no feeling, powered by senseless villainy and over-the-top theatrics. Upon release, You Only Live Once was a limp entry to the franchise, but today it is a bitterly hard-to-watch mishit that serves as a painstaking procession of every nasty trope and tendency the original Bond pictures had.

2006’s Casino Royale is a true masterpiece of action cinema, slick sophistication, and gripping high-stakes drama that finds the perfect balance between exhilarating set piece and character-charged intensity. The 1967 interpretation of the Bond story, however, is not. The unlicensed Bond adaptation follows a retired 007 (David Niven) as he is forced to re-enter the field to bring down the evil international crime faction SMERSH, which has been behind a recent series of deadly attacks on MI6 operatives. In an effort to mislead the criminal syndicate, several others also pose as agent 007, including baccarat master Evelyn Tremble (Peter Sellers) and Bond’s own former secretary, Miss Moneypenny (Barbara Bouchet).

The idea of lampooning the spy genre was good in theory, but the execution of 1967’s Casino Royale leaves much to be desired. Its story is a chaotic mess that is completely incomprehensible and never comes close to filling the film’s bloated 131-minute runtime, while on-set conflicts saw the movie pulled in several different directions, making the final product intangible. Even a supporting cast including Orson Welles, Woody Allan, and original Bond girl Ursula Andress are incapable of elevating the film beyond its pitiful nature. It was admonished by the masses upon release, and it has only gotten worse over the years.

The Bond franchise has had its fair share of mishits over the decades, but none have been quite so disastrous and agonizing as 2002’s Die Another Day. It marked an unfortunate end to Pierce Brosnan’s tenure as 007, which started out so well with GoldenEye giving a clear intent of suave style and gritty action. Three films later, the Bond saga had regressed to uninspiring uncertainty. Die Another Day is an awkward, disjointed conglomerate of the litany of Bond styles that came before it, and every tonal shift and plot twist it aspires for falls flat on its face.

The opening sequence has a certain gruffness to it, with Bond being tortured by the North Korean army over the course of 14 months, but whatever intrigue that hard-edged intro may have had immediately dissipates as the movie pivots to cringe-worthy campiness. Not only is Die Another Day’s narrative tempo off beat, its reliance on appalling CGI and ridiculous concepts to carry some of its action sequences is enough to leave viewers in hysterics. It marks an undisputed low-point for the franchise, a painful depiction of 007 at its absolute worst. The only saving grace of the movie is that it was so bad it forced producers to take an entirely new approach four years later when the saga was re-ignited with Casino Royale.

Sony Pictures has won the services to one of the most in-demand commercial directors working today, Shawn Levy. Levy and his 21 Laps banner have signed a major first look overall film deal with Sony Pictures, with Sony beating out multiple studios in what’s said to be a competitive process.

Levy will develop and produce theatrical films through the 21 Laps Entertainment banner as part of the deal, which begins fall 2027 and extends across all Sony Pictures labels, so presumably that could include labels like Screen Gems or even Sony Animation. It’s a producing deal, not for directing, but we wouldn’t be surprised if that ends up being the case with one that his team brings in. This film deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps as recently as September signed a new overall TV deal with Disney’s 20th Television, with him exiting his Netflix deal. That pact doesn’t begin until October 2027.

Levy is reuniting with Sony’s leadership Tom Rothman and Sanford Panitch after he previously directed the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen,” and “Date Night” for them while they were all at Fox.

“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group Chairman and CEO Tom Rothman said in a statement. “His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative company around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm. I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”

“Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy said in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a bighearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful. 21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”

While just about everyone else in Hollywood has taken a victory lap with the success of “Backrooms,” you may have forgotten that Levy and 21 Laps were producers on the A24 horror movie, and he of course directed and produced Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” which concluded at the end of last year. Up next for Levy is “Star Wars: Starfighter,” which is a “Star Wars” spinoff starring Ryan Gosling and which opens May 28, 2027. And he’s also teaming with Gosling and Disney yet again on Marvel’s “Ghost Rider,” which opens July 28, 2028. His last feature he directed was “Deadpool & Wolverine,” which made $1.3 billion worldwide.

On the 21 Laps side, the banner is producing a rom-com with Emma Stone and Chris Pine set at Universal called “The Catch;” Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons;” Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.

Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

#3348. Where to find the Port Gellhorn serial killer in GTA 6

Three missing person cases can only mean one thing...

Three missing person cases can only mean one thing...

Finding Port Gelhorn's missing tourists and the serial killer in Grand Theft Auto 6 takes you on a twisted journey around the town, one with few guideposts and a lot of chances to get stuck. It's a macabre scavenger hunt with only a few pictures and knowledge of the surrounding area to go by, though the reward at the end is comparatively small. This is a quest where the storytelling, more than anything else, is the reward.

Below, we explain where to find Gelhorn's missing tourists in GTA 6 and complete the serial killer side mission.

You'll first come across this exploration mission in the Starlet Motel office after Chapter 2 starts. Lucia can examine a set of missing persons posters on the wall next to Linda's desk. There's a tip line with a number to call, but it just takes you to a voice mailbox.

And that's the only hint to go off of, as the poster info gives you no clues and nowhere to look. There might be other clues hidden somewhere around town, but we didn't find them. Instead, we stumbled across the quest's starting location by accident. It's an old bunker-like warehouse across the street from Moses' garage, next to the scooter store. You can approach the front for a prompt to open the door, but it won't work. Walk down the right side of the warehouse, and look for a hole at the base. Crawl inside.

Despite how creepy the location is, there's nothing inside to harm you, though there is a jump scare midway through. Enter the red room and the trophy room beyond it, and interact with the photos there. You'll see locations showing each of the missing tourists, and these photos are stored in your phone gallery if you want to view them later. The quest prompt changes in the map menu, too, with a new prompt for each photo.

You can track them in any order. We're just listing them in the order we found them. We recommend tackling this part of the quest during the day, just so it's easier to make out landmarks.

The junkyard is where you'll find Susanne Keeble, and it's next to the Pay 'n' Spray shop in central Gelhorn. You're looking for a pink car, and if you're having trouble finding it, activate focus mode. The car will stand out as the only interactable object in the area. Report the body to the tip line after you find it.

Donald Miller's body is out at Wild Hog Point, the marshes outside Port Gelhorn. Head toward the tree with no leaves near the center of the marsh, and look in the water nearby to find a car. Interact with it, report the body, and move on. Someone picks up the line this time.

Patrick Murray is the final tourist, and his body is in a trailer at the far north end of Port Gelhorn in an abandoned trailer park near a water tower. The trailer in question is the blue one. Head inside, and pull up the floorboards near the door to discover Murray's body. The clipping in the trophy room mentioned a reward for information about him, though, for reasons you'll soon discover, the tip line operator isn't ready to pay out.

The tip line man asks you to return to the warehouse after finding the third body, and the quest can change depending on whether you go alone or with your partner. We played as Jason and went with Lucia, though who takes the lead doesn't matter. Your partner stays outside, and tense events unfold inside, after which the culprit dies and the quest ends. You can grab the killer's glasses as a unique "found" accessory for Jason if you want.

If you're just getting started in GTA 6, we have plenty of guides to help you live the high life in Leonida. Check out our GTA 6 beginner guide to get a grasp of the basics and our tips for what to do first, recommendations for the best ways to make money fast, and an explainer for how to keep stolen weapons and cars to make the most of your free time.
