#3347. 10 Mad Magazine Mascot Alfred P. Neuman Quotes To Live By

The humor periodical Mad started off as a comic in 1952, before taking on its more recognizable magazine with 1955's Mad #24. That cover featured a prominent appearance by the caricature of a character who would come to be known as Alfred E. Neuman. A few issues later, on the cover of Mad #30, Alfred took center stage, officially becoming the magazine's figurehead and mascot.

From its inception, issues of Mad included an epigraph, a quote from a historical figure, politician, or celebrity that set the tone. The first time Mad opened with a quote attributed to Alfred E. Neuman was Mad #38. From that point on, Alfred has had the first, and definitive, line in practically every issue of the magazine since.

Sometimes Alfred's quotes are bawdy, and sometimes they are politically charged. Often, though, they are low-key life lessons, the kind of wisdom that only a comic character can get away with sharing.

"It's a good idea to keep your words soft and sweet because you never know when you'll have to eat them!" Here, Alfred E. Neuman riffs on a centuries-old idiom. Be careful what comes out of your mouth, Neuman warns, because if what you say ends up getting shoved back in your face, down your own throat, you might find yourself choking on the tone and the meanings of your words.

It is sensible advice, especially for comedians, but knowing Alfred, and knowing Mad magazine, this is really a "do as I say, not as I do" case of cautionary advice.

"You'll never get rid of a bad temper by losing it!" There's another saying, which is that you can't control your immediate reaction to something, but you can control your reaction to the reaction. If you're prone to getting angry, giving into it is only going to make the problem worse, that's what Alfred E. Neuman is saying here.

It is a slyly clever bit of wordplay. In fact, this bon mot could be remixed into a riddle. "What can you never get rid of by losing it?" "A bad temper!" The cover for this issue, Mad #71, shows Alfred's mug at the center of a dartboard, and with its opening quote at least, the magazine hit the comedic bullseye.

"Learn from the mistakes of others." That is age-old wisdom. But why? That part is usually left unsaid, but leave it to Alfred E. Neuman to say the quiet part loud. It is "'cause you'll never live long enough to make 'em all yourself!"

Before it was a film franchise, National Lampoon was a groundbreaking American humor magazine; these are the greatest covers from its 3-decade history

Life is finite. There's only so much failure and foible the average person can cram into one lifetime. Recognizing and avoiding others' failures isn't about being more likely to succeed in your own endeavors. It is simply a time-saving exercise. Plus, in some cases, those mistakes might have been fatal, and avoiding them is the only way to guarantee a long life full non-lethal errors in judgment.

The art of the one-liner is trickier than people give it credit for. (Just ask Henny Youngman.) In just a few words, the speaker has to set up and execute the punchline, but there is more to it than that. The line has to conjure an image in people's heads. And that image can be vague, or it can be concrete.

Here, it is literally the latter. "Some minds are like concrete," Alfred E. Neuman says in Mad #82, in the sense that they are "all mixed up and permanently set." In other words, some people are defiantly confused. Obstinately misguided. Flat out wrong and unwilling to revise their opinions. Don't be like those people, Alfred suggests. Be willing to admit your wrong.

Long before Gordan Gecko told the world "greed is good" in Wall Street, Alfred E. Neuman gave Mad readers the real truth about cold hard cash. "Sometimes, the best scheme for doubling your money is to fold it in half and stuff it back in your wallet," Neuman declared in Mad #87.

Meaning, get-rich-quick schemes and seemingly lucrative investments are often not all they seemed cracked up to be. Everyone wants to hustle, and maximize their earnings, but sometimes the smart thing to do is just stack paper. Save up. For Alfred, a folded dollar is worth more than one that is tied up in escrow.

The funny thing about Alfred E. Neuman's advice is that he was often both the angel and the devil on readers' shoulders. His line in Mad #145 exemplifies this. "Sometimes it pays to resist a temptation," he begins. Sounds totally reasonable, and also morally sound, right?

Well, let him finish. Because Alfred also answers why it pays. Not because having will power and self-control are important. Not because resisting temptation is the right thing. No, because temptation is a gamble. Why take the one in front of you when "a better one may be coming along." This hilariously, and cheekily, takes the matter from an ethical equation to a practical matter of when it is the right time to do the wrong thing.

"Experience is something you never have until just after you need it!" This quote from Mad #204 is the perfect companion to the issue's cover, which parodies the Jaws 2 poster, with Alfred E. Neuman piloting a mechanical shark to sneak up on a jet-skiing girl in a bikini.

In the movie, only Chief Brody has the ability to save the day, because only he has the experience of having fought a killer great white before. For most people, most of the time, the toughest moments of their lives are trial and error, giving them the experience that would have made it easier on them only after the fact.

This quote from Mad #221 evokes the earlier entry on this list from Mad #54. It is another way for Alfred E. Neuman to remind readers: "Watch what you say." Especially if you've already gotten yourself in trouble by talking too much.

"When you're in deep water, it's a good idea to keep your mouth shut!" It is a great case of applying a literal lesson to figurative language. If you're in proverbial deep water, or hot water, or any kind of water, talking, or shouting, is only going to result in one thing. Drowning.

Mad #267's cover features a Top Gun parody, and Alfred E. Neuman's quote in the issue makes it clear what kind of people he'd like to strap to the nose of a fighter jet and send flying. "People on ego trips," who, Alfred says bluntly, "should buy one-way tickets."

It is a slick play on words, but the point doesn't mince any. If you are ego-driven and willing to do whatever it takes to feed your own sense of self, take a hike. Take a vacation. Take off and don't come back. For Mad fans, it is a reminder to check themselves before they wreck themselves, and ruin someone else's day too.

The theme of Mad #293's Alfred E. Neuman quote is the same as the prior entry. And it contains essentially the same valuable life lesson. Which is, life is hard for everyone, so don't go around making it harder.

Or as Alfred puts it: "It's not just the ups and downs that make life difficult. It's the jerks." People who go around being miserable all the time need to do more than just sit down and read a Mad magazine, or a Far Side comic, or even a Garfield, and try to lighten up. They need to think about how they are impacting other people. That's what Mad's irreverent, but often on-point mascot is saying here.

#3346. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3345. ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question

Don’t let the title fool you: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” might offer up a breezy, very fun-to-watch new entry into the life and times of titular (and fictitious) Hollywood stuntman, but co-star Elizabeth Debicki steals the show in David Fincher’s film (in addition to stealing the heart of Brad Pitt’s Cliff). Is it time to greenlight “The New Adventures of Karen Crosby”? We think so.

The much-anticipated sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon in Hollywood” picks up nearly a decade after the Oscar-winning antics of the previous film, finding Cliff pursuing new professional endeavors (film projecting! bartending! contract killing, kind of!). Stunt work? Eh, only when he feels like, and he certainly feels like after taking an unexpected meeting with Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Debicki), whose grace and good humor instantly delight both Cliff and the audience. Related Stories Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script

Tossed together by the wacky demands of Karen’s marquee client, actor Charlie Nelson (Scott Caan), the shaggy, Tarantino-penned “Cliff Booth” meanders its way through every corner of Hollywood, finding real emotional ballast and crackling chemistry every time Pitt and Debicki share the screen. Characteristically wordy and dense, we learn plenty about Karen along the way (including her early forays into film criticism and her current feelings about movies), and she wins Cliff’s heart by, well, literally and physically slapping the crap out of him.

Ahead, IndieWire catches up with the Aussie star (who gets to use her real accent this time) about Fincher’s film, from slapping her co-star to some serious ruminations on the instantly iconic “pig monologue speech.” No wonder Cliff went so crazy for Karen; she’s a delight.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: What was your relationship with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” when the film came out in 2019?

Elizabeth Debicki: I went to see it in the cinema. I think I went by myself, which makes me think I must have been on a job. I was definitely in the States, maybe I was in L.A., and I went one afternoon. I went and sat in the cinema, and I loved it. It’s really vivid in my memory.

I didn’t watch it again before we made this for performance reasons. In a way, I realized I didn’t really need to because, [there’s] something about Quentin’s movies, they just kind of wedge themselves in your brain. I can literally see the Playboy Mansion scene. I can see the Manson kids driving up to the house. I can see Margaret Qualley’s feet on the dashboard. I can see everything.

So it sounds like you came into this as a Tarantino fan.

And to get Tarantino and Fincher is this incredible two-for-one.

It’s funny, because obviously in the making of this, I had to sort of normalize that. And they helped me do that because they were, from the second I got onto set — which was a two-week rehearsal period where we really worked through the script — we had Quentin for that whole period. [It was] very, very collaborative.

A part of me wonders whether it was that thing where they have sat with the material for so long and had their full body relationship to it, and then I was fresh. I had my own thoughts and feelings. My memories of those rehearsal periods were really all three of them [Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt] just turning to me and saying, “What do you think? What do you think?” The first time it happened, I was like, “Oh my God, what do I think?” After a little while, I started to actually say what I thought, which was great.

I didn’t audition for this. David emailed me and asked me if I would be interested in playing a part. I remember he phrased it in an email as he hoped that I would consider playing a very tricky part in a film he was hoping to make in July. It was a very David-ism kind of email. I think it said something like, “I hope you understand the seriousness of this conundrum,” or something. And I called him up and yeah, I was obviously ready to say, “I’ll do it.”

He was very, very insistent. He was like, “Wait, wait, wait. I really want to tell you everything about it.” Because at that point he and Quentin were doing a massive edit of the script. He couldn’t send it to me there and then.

Karen is so singular, but she is in a familiar position if you’re working in Hollywood. Did you base any part of your performance on any agents or managers or publicists that you know or have encountered?

When I first read the script, there were things that just rang so true to me, and might seem outrageous for anyone or slightly absurd maybe for anyone who doesn’t work in this industry. The incredible pig scene where Cliff talks about killing a pig, and then the scene in the car where Karen says, “Now because of you, I now have to spend my entire morning finding a pig. That is not a joke, that is literally what I have to get up and do. And you know what? I had a lot of things I had to do, and it wasn’t find a pig. And now I have to drive your ass all the way to Marina del Rey because I have to just deliver you because that’s what my client needed.”

It’s kind of this absurd ask, but it’s folded into “that’s what I need for my process.” Quentin and David, they’re so fascinating because they are Hollywood. They are Hollywood, and also they sit outside it, and they observe it from these very, very unique vantage points. Quentin, in particular, his love affair with L.A. is so profound, and with Hollywood. Part of the thing I loved about her too is that she’s sort of accidentally an agent, which is not frequently do you come across that. One of the things too that feels very human about her is that she sort of had this other dream, but she took one really bad knock, and it broke her heart, and she just buried it deep inside and then made decisions based off that.

When we get to that scene with Karen and Cliff when you’re talking about how Karen had this other career as a film critic, I how much of that was lifted from what would’ve been Quentin’s movie, “The Movie Critic”?

I don’t know. I don’t actually know the answer to that question in terms of the parallel there. But I do love that in the middle of this film about 1977 in Hollywood, that there’s a really important moment where we think about Pauline Kael, and we think about her and she lives in this film. I’m so glad that there’s this moment where my character gets to say, “Pauline Kael is my god,” because she was. She was incredible.

As Karen, you have this great monologue explaining to Cliff who you used to be, what had happened with that career path, how wonderful it was that Pauline supported you, and then it didn’t work out. And then you have another monologue about seeing movies as hamburgers. It’s a really funny tension for Karen, because the audience likely assumes she loves movies and does see them as art.

That’s right, there is a tension there. I feel like one of the things that Quentin can do so well, and kind of totally unique to his own brain, is that he sort of plucks an idea out of the zeitgeist, something that we’re all thinking about, and he feeds it through his characters in a way that feels very organic. This is a big conversation that people are having as the industry shifts and changes. It also was a huge conversation that was happening in 1977. There was this big question of, “Is that art still if it’s commercial, if its box office success equates to this?” I think that the dichotomy of what she believes in her heart and wants to be true and what she spouts in front of people, I sort of think both things are true at once, and I think that’s just the kind of human element.

But I also think that it’s important to remember in that monologue that Charlie really pulls it out of her. She really doesn’t want to do the dance, the dancing monkey, or what did she say? “There’s a dancing bear aspect to your request,” I think is such a great line. But yeah, I think both things are true for her.

You have the sense she’s said this speech before, and again, maybe she doesn’t totally believe it, but Charlie just loves it and so she has to do it.

David and I spoke about it a lot, and we sort of landed on we feel like she did it once off the cuff, like at a table at the Emmys or the Globes, and everyone went, “Gee, Karen, that’s genius.” And Charlie heard it and went, “Yeah, that’s genius. She’s my agent, look how smart she is. She’s so great.” Then she’s done it one other time at a dinner. So, by the time we get to the pool, she’s like, “Oh, my God.” It’s becoming a routine against her will, which was also a really fun element to play with in terms of how much she does or doesn’t enjoy it, and finding that balance.

Do you personally read reviews of your work?

Has it always been the case? [Smiles] I’m sure anyone who doesn’t read a review once read a bad review.

It doesn’t even have to be a bad one. What I learned is, you can read a review that is seemingly positive, but it might not be what you were trying to do, and then you feel heartbroken about that too. So yes, I really avoid it. Yeah.

You get to slap Brad Pitt a lot in this film. Was that hard to do?

It’s a very beautiful face, and we had to do it. We had to do it. And Brad is a very good sport and a very good stuntman. I think that Brad was very, very comfortable, and I was very nervous. We shot the dialogue for two days, that we were just in almost this sort of trance of the two of them, and of the very unusual power dynamic that [they have]. One of the best things about that scene to me, which I didn’t analyze at the time, it’s so intricate the way that Quentin wrote it. It’s this moment where, in revealing what he wants, he becomes so vulnerable that the power dynamic kind of very subtly shifts in this kind of core foundational way between these two characters.

So, we shot that for two days and then all of a sudden it was like, “Oh, my God, it ends, and I need to figure out how to do this.” We had an amazing stunt coordinator on that job.

We had to do extremely complex things with people, but with me, I was like, “Hey Dave, could we just pop out the back there and have a little chat about the slap…?”

Everyone knows that David likes to do a lot of takes. How many takes was the actual slapping?

Not so many! It was probably the least amount of takes we did. We probably did a couple, five, maybe six. And then I do remember that Brad sort of went, “OK, I think we got it. I think we’re good now,” and we moved on. But we did the inside [slap] first. It was such a joy to do. It’s such a happy memory. We filmed it, and then we all ran around to the monitor, and we watched it in playback, and we’re like, “Oh, my God, it’s so good.” And then we filmed it again. We were so pleased with ourselves. [Laughs]

What scenes did David ask for the most takes?

The thing about the takes is, it’s coverage-dependent. So, if you have four actors in a scene, like the hamburger monologue, let’s say there’s four setups on each actor, you do 10 takes per setup. So, that becomes a lot.

I will say that in the pig speech monologue, I don’t have a lot of lines, but we did just as much coverage on me as we did on Brad and Scott. That was one of my first days on set, and I remember thinking, “This is so, so unusual. Why is he doing this?” And then a couple weeks later, he showed me a kind of rough edit, and I thought, “Oh, my God, that’s why he did it.” He is using Karen as the kind of go-between. As David would always say, at least there’s one grown-up in the room, and it’s Karen.

So I do have this really funny memory too of doing that during the pig monologue scene. I was off-camera, or we were catching just the side of me; I was very much out of focus, and I took a drag of the cigarette, and I remember he gave me a note for that, something about the speed of it or the intention of it. And I remember thinking …

Exactly! I was like, “You saw that?” And he was right, he was absolutely right, but I thought, “OK, this is not a set where we get away with anything.”

Especially in that scene, you have these facial expressions where you are having the appropriate reaction to what we’re hearing, but in such a beautiful way. I think that’s when we all fall in love with Karen. We’re like, “She gets it. She knows how ridiculous this is,” but she is part of this world.

I’m particularly proud of the Tic Tac crunch; that was my prop idea, and I just thought we should end with her crunching down on something, because she’s so pissed about having to then go and spend her entire morning looking for a hog in Malibu Colony or something. Where is she even going to find that pig?

She did it. I mean, David and I would talk about that too. I’m like, “Do you think she did it or she sent Mallory, her assistant, to go do it?” Either way, someone did it, someone paid for it.

Speaking of falling in love with Karen, there’s been this sentiment circulating as people see the film that there is a real rom-com built into it with Cliff and Karen. Do you see it that way?

I don’t think it’s a rom-com, but I think it’s romantic, and I think they’re funny. Don’t get me wrong, rom-coms are my religion. Yesterday I was walking through New York, and I literally felt like I was in “You’ve Got Mail.” I was like, “This fall day, I need a bunch of sharpened pencils.” But I don’t think that this necessarily falls into that category. It’s sort of undefinable, indefinable, but I do think it’s really romantic. I felt that when we were playing it, and we really enjoyed that together.

The romance of it is kind of surprising, because it surprises her. It’s sort of best case scenario romance, that you think you have it all together, and this person walks in that you absolutely dismiss in terms of that, and then little by little they just sort of reveal this thing. More beautifully, they pull something out of you. I didn’t necessarily intellectualize any of this while we were shooting it, it’s just that I can see that now retrospectively. Not that I read anything, but I am curious what people will make of them.

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3344. ‘NCIS’ Star Teases Potential Ziva Return After Spin-Off Cancellation

NCIS has been welcoming back a ton of familiar faces from across the franchise throughout this fall. The two biggest, however, have been Mark Harmon jumping back in front of the camera for a third season of NCIS: Origins that puts an older Gibbs back in the line of fire, and Michael Weatherly rejoining his old colleagues at the Washington Navy Yard as Tony DiNozzo. Following the end of NCIS: Tony & Ziva on Paramount+, the latter is set up for a longer return to the flagship series after moving back into the area to establish a new office for his security company and instead landing an entirely new job as the new director of NCIS in place of the late Leon Vance (Rocky Carroll). Because of that, it feels inevitable that Ziva David (Cote de Pablo) will eventually make an appearance too.

As the series explains, Tony's longtime love interest is just a stone's throw away, with their daughter Tali attending boarding school in Boston. However, showrunner Steven D. Binder previously ruled out a return in Season 24, meaning an on-screen reunion between the couple after their spin-off's cancelation isn't imminent. Still, the groundwork is set for her to join the team on a mission like old times at a moment's notice. One person who has long been waiting for that opportunity is Katrina Law, who feels it's more a matter of when than if she steps back into the field.

Law recently spoke to Cinemablend about how Season 24 was unfolding so far and was questioned about the possibility of a guest appearance by de Pablo. Jessica Knight has a particular connection to Ziva, as it's revealed the two are directly in contact to keep tabs on Tony and his diet while he's at work. For Law, that fully opens the door to a future Knight and Ziva mission that'll allow the two women to combine their skills both as highly trained special agents and in driving Tony crazy. "I fully expect Ziva to come onto our show and Knight and Ziva team up and just make Weatherly extremely uncomfortable, but then go off and, like, have a massive fight scene together to take down some bad guy."

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Weatherly was initially brought aboard for a season-long arc for Season 24, but the fact that he's the team's new man in the chair seems to indicate his return as Tony isn't just a brief visit. He's working well with the current team, from Knight to his old pal McGee (Sean Murray), and the former agent even got to reunite with his old boss during a poignant crossover with NCIS: Origins. Binder, for his part, is loving having an NCIS legend back in the fold, though he previously shared that they're taking things "one season at a time" as far as the story and Weatherly go. "Certainly, it’s been really great having him in that chair, and I don’t see any reason why it should slow, but I don’t know that we’re looking quite that far yet." It seems the hope would be for Tony to stick around a while in a recurring role, making the chances of Ziva returning to D.C. in Season 25 or beyond all the more likely.

NCIS Season 24 is off this week, with new episodes picking up on Tuesday, December 1. Stay tuned here at Collider for more news and updates on the long-running procedural.

#3343. Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens

The Big Game is coming to the Big Screen. Technically the biggest screens.

Super Bowl LXI is set to play live on IMAX screens across North America, as well as in some international markets, specifically Australia, New Zealand, and Brazil. The game takes place on Sunday, February 14, 2027, or Valentine’s Day 2027, and now you can convince your partner that the Valentine’s Day date night is still alive because you can go out to the movie theater to watch the game instead of stay at home.

IMAX will screen everything from the pregame and postgame coverage, the full four-hour presentation of the game itself, and of course the Halftime Show headlined by Jay-Z, all beginning at 6 pm ET. ESPN’s Monday Night Football broadcast team of Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters, and Laura Rutledge will be the ones you hear in the theater, so no luck if you’re a Peyton and Eli or Pat McAfee fan. The only thing we don’t know is who’s playing in the game just yet, but this Chicago Bears fan is feeling pretty good about his team’s chances. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures

Tickets are expected to go on sale in January. Specific theater locations and ticketing information will be announced in the coming weeks.

This is the first time IMAX is screening something as big as the Super Bowl, but it’s not the first time IMAX has played live sporting events in its theaters. IMAX also screened the opening ceremony for the Paris Olympics, it this year did a series of F1 races in partnership with Apple TV, and events like NHL games and even the NBA Finals have played internationally. This is on a much bigger scale as well, as this will be available in hundreds of IMAX screens across the country.

ABC, Disney, and ESPN hadn’t been in the rotation for the Super Bowl for a long time, so they’ve been going all out for their first go around. Disney is making the game available via broadcast on ABC, as well as on ESPN and Univision, and also for streaming on Disney+. ESPN is also doing an alternate telecast on ESPN 2 with Peyton and Eli Manning as they do for “Monday Night Football” throughout the regular season. And it was previously announced that “The Pat McAfee Show” is getting in on the fun with its own Super Bowl show on ESPNU and “Playbook with Next Gen Stats” on NFL Network.

This is really a boon for theaters to do added business on a day and weekend when most theaters are pretty empty and the new movie options are few and far between. We’ll see though how the box office responds and how many people relocate their Super Bowl parties to their local multiplex.

“Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and IMAX takes it to a historic new scale,” said Ken Potrock, President, Major Event Integration for The Walt Disney Company. “With ESPN’s first Super Bowl, we’re reaching fans across an unprecedented range of platforms and meeting them wherever they want to be, with unique moments that only Disney and ESPN can deliver.”

“The Super Bowl is a one-of-a-kind global cultural event imbued with spectacle, sound, drama, and heroes — all the makings of a great IMAX experience,” said Rich Gelfond, CEO of IMAX. “This is a milestone for IMAX that further elevates our standing as a premier global platform for entertainment and events, and we’re excited to work in partnership with Disney, ESPN and the NFL to give football fans an unforgettable night.”

#3342. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3341. Legendary Critical Role Cast Members Officially Return With a Star-Studded New Guest Cast

Aabria Iyengar and Travis Willingham return in Campaign 4

It’s hard to believe the entire Critical Role table for Campaign 4 hasn’t been together since the Convergence arc in June. Since then, the Soldiers, Seekers, and Schemers tables have remained separate. Or, more accurately, the Seekers and Schemers tables have remained separate.

Since Critical Role Campaign 4 episode 31, "Trick of the Light," Critters haven’t seen hide nor hair of everyone’s favorite orc Druid, Thaisha Lloy. Nor have they received any confirmation about when, exactly, Travis Willingham will return with a new character, after his Paladin, Teor Pridesire, met an unfortunate end in episode 30, "Here in the Dark."

Luckily, the wait is finally over. Critical Role announced on Nov. 23 that its eagerly anticipated Soldiers table, featuring Aabria Iyengar as Thaisha, will return on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10 for a two-part Soldiers table arc. And she won’t be alone.

When the three tables split off in June last year, it seemed that the Soldiers table would consist only of Thaisha. In an interview with Polygon, Iyengar confirmed she wasn't sure at the time whether Thaisha’s story would be told through cold openings or off-camera. Later, however, the Critical Role team decided to give the Soldiers table a mini-arc following Thaisha as she explored her future on the druidic path. But she would not be doing all of that on her own.

“We’ve got some amazing guests, Celia Rose Gooding and Abubakar Salim," Iyengar told Polygon. "Two people who I have admired for so long; it was so fun to finally sit down and play with them. And, of course, the return of Travis Willingham and his new PC.”

Willingham has been absent from Critical Role’s Campaign 4 since his katari Paladin, Teor Pridesire, died in episode 30. Teor was killed inside House Tachonis’s Obrimus Manor during a truly heartbreaking moment for the fans and the cast.

Gooding and Salim have both guest-starred on Critical Role before: Gooding appeared in Exandria Unlimited: Divergence as the half-elf Rei’nia Saph, while Salim has played various roles, most recently the fungril Berserker Mercy in Age of Umbra: Sallowlands.

Though Iyengar couldn’t reveal what characters Willingham and the other guests would play in this two-episode arc, she told Polygon they were all “deeply connected and bound by a similar purpose.”

“Dol-Runja is the seat of the orcs and the druids in Kahan. So it's important and interesting to see multiple facets of that.”

Since June, the Seekers and Schemers tables have been dealing with assassination attempts at the theater, watery heists, and literal hell. When we last checked in, the Seekers table — with the help of several NPCs like fey pixie Clauny the Rose, talking dog Dame Morgaine, and scoundrel Pimley Morn — successfully rescued their ally turned into stone, Ulbid Morn.

On Dec. 3, Critters will reunite with Thaisha, who set off for the city of Dol-Rungja. There, she hopes to speak with the Druidic people and persuade them to abandon their neutrality and help fight back against the Sundered Houses.

Whether that will work out for Thaisha remains to be seen. The last time she encountered other druids, a few of them weren’t too pleased with her role in bringing the Necromancer Wizard, Occtis Tachonis (Alexander Ward), back to life as a Hollowed One. Given that she’ll have to answer for it to very important people, including her grandma, we expect the orc druid to be put through the proverbial wringer over the course of her two-episode arc.

Aabria Iyengar, Travis Willingham, and guest stars Celia Rose Gooding and Abubakar Salim begin their Soldiers adventure on Dec. 3.

#3340. Netflix's 8-Part Hard Sci-Fi Series Is Already Renewed For 2 More Seasons

While there are a lot of great original sci-fi shows to come out of Netflix over the years, only one has preemptively avoided a major industry issue with its two-season renewal. It’s a tale as old as time. Viewers are only just getting into a new series, often an ambitious genre show with sci-fi, fantasy, or horror elements, when it is abruptly canceled despite critical acclaim.

From HBO’s one-season wonder Lovecraft Country to the iconic space western Firefly, there is no shortage of promising shows that were unexpectedly ended early by shock cancellations. Often, this leaves their storylines frustratingly unfinished, and fans end up feeling short-changed no matter how much money might have been spent on the budget of these shows during their runs. One need only look at Prime Video’s fantasy series The Wheel of Time for another example.

While the Robert Jordan adaptation was consistently critically adored throughout its three-season run, the show’s abrupt ending arrived long before the series had adapted the entire literary saga to the small screen. As such, what had felt like three increasingly promising seasons of fantasy TV ended up seeming instead like a lot of buildups to nothing. This is why it is so exciting to hear that Netflix’s 3 Body Problem has already avoided this issue with a preemptive two-season renewal.

Based on Chinese novelist Liu Cixin’s trilogy of books Remembrance of Earth's Past, 3 Body Problem’s title came from a real-life Newtonian physics problem. Fittingly enough, 3 Body Problem’s plot focused on a group of scientific researchers from different disciplines, dubbed the “Oxford Five,” coming together to investigate the mysterious deaths of their fellow academics. Eventually, the group unmask a secret conspiracy involving a cult and alien fleets that are preparing to invade earth.

Only, that’s not quite an accurate summary, since 3 Body Problem’s depiction of first contact with extraterrestrial life isn’t as simple as invasions or attacks. Unlike the earlier underrated TNT sci-fi series Falling Skies, 3 Body Problem’s extraterrestrials aren’t straightforward sentient, corporeal creatures, and their plans for earth aren’t as obvious as world domination or the intentional, malicious destruction of human civilization.

Instead, 3 Body Problem’s story merges the past, the present, virtual realities, and layered versions of its story told from different perspectives to create a rich, complex character-driven saga. 3 Body Problem is undoubtedly an odyssey, mixing the ambitious scope of earlier genre shows like The Walking Dead, The Expanse, or Game of Thrones with the narrative complexity of Westworld or Lost.

Despite this ambition, 3 Body Problem doesn’t end up overextending itself in its first outing, and the show is now guaranteed to make it to the end of its source story without needing to rush through the plot at a rate of knots. Where earlier Netflix sci-fi shows like Stranger Things expanded their once-modest stories to become ever more commodious and elaborate, 3 Body Problem was always a complicated show.

Luckily, however, Netflix renewed 3 Body Problem for seasons 2 and 3, ensuring the show has sufficient screen time to adapt the remainder of the source novel series. This is particularly reassuring for fans of Remembrance of Earth's Past since, while the novel was celebrated at the time of its release, Liu Cixin’s books were also thought to be unfilmable due to their unique structure.

3 Body Problem needed to reorder events and rejig characters, while still maintaining the same central plot, and pulled this off with aplomb in season 1. However, it is only since Netflix’s renewal that viewers can be reassured 3 Body Problem will be able to stick the show's landing.

#3338. How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder

Editor’s Note: This article contains spoilers for “Minotaur.”

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev has worked with supervising re-recording mixer Andrey Dergachev for 20 years, since the director’s second film, “Banishment.” On each project, including their most recent portrait of a rotten marriage in a rotten world, “Minotaur,” they’ve tried to improve the sound design—using it as a hook that makes the film’s world feel more vital and alive for the audience.

Seriously, spoilers. This is never more true than in the absurdly sad and funny, then suddenly murderous confrontation between cuckolded husband Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) and his wife’s lover Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk) at the hinge point of “Minotaur.” Related Stories Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question

Zvyagintsev and Dergachev generally strive to preserve as much authentic production sound from performances as possible. “On my third movie, ‘Elena,’ we recorded the live sound from shooting, and it’s maybe two or three phrases we had to rerecord, but otherwise the whole sound that you hear is fully recorded during the shooting,” Zvyagintsev told IndieWire on an upcoming episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “Our main purpose is to keep as much sound from the shooting as possible and not to add anything extra, and it was the same for ‘Minotaur.’”

But for the moment that Gleb attacks Anton, and its aftermath, it was important to Zvyagintsev that the world beyond the apartment start intruding on Gleb — that even though he wants desperately to cover up what he’s done and make sure no one sees or learns about it, we hear dozens of ways in which he isn’t alone. That required a lot of work outside of the studio to record the background noises Zvyagintsev and Dergachev could then layer into the scene.

“We were creating [background] sounds of the kids playing football in the backyard. We would spend the whole day recording the kids, how they’re speaking, the way they’re playing, people passing by on the street,” Zvyagintsev said. They also recorded different sound layers from Gleb’s luxury SUV, which they could deploy to create maximum panic in both Gleb and the audience.

“The car signals, the leaves on the street, the birds — they all pronounced, and [emphasized] something. So we were modulating all those layers that we recorded, and then we combined them to create the atmosphere and to put it all in one place for the scene,” Zvyagintsev said.

There’s atmosphere from outside and from inside, as Zvyagintsev and Dergachev refused to let Gleb have a moment of peace on the soundtrack — until, as with all the cruel jokes of “Minotaur’s” filmmaking, he gets it in the worst way, at the worst possible moment. There’s a terrible silence once he’s struck Anton on the head with his own camera. And then the world comes rushing back in, even louder than before.

“We were trying to create this volume of sounds right after the hit. And then, when Anton is falling, there is this complete silence. And then somewhere far away we hear the car alarm and even more sounds that create this volume. This is what we were looking for,” Zvyagintsev said.

It was important to finesse the sound design of the sequence so as not to overplay it. Zvyagintsev initially wanted to add music to the moment, but had to hold himself back. “It was really tempting,” Zvyagintsev said. “My composer Evgueni Galperine even wrote the music, which we added. But when we saw the result, we realized, and I understood that no, no, it has to be completely silent.”

Silent as the grave, one might say. But it’s the sound design, the modulation between loudness and silence, that makes the moment so horrifying. Zvyagintsev and Dergachev did it by hand, just to make sure of it.

“Minotaur” is now playing in select theaters.

#3337. The 6 Most Outrageous GTA 6 Myths, Debunked

The internet is already drowning in GTA 6 misinformation

After a wild opening weekend, Grand Theft Auto 6 is off to the races. Millions are playing Rockstar’s enormous open-world game and discovering its complexities in real time. There’s a lot to unpack in a game that’s filled with intersecting gameplay systems across a long story, and some players are already taking advantage of that. At the same time, the opening days of GTA 6’s launch have been filled with misinformation, much of it fueled by culture warriors and content creators looking to turn outrage into clicks on social media platforms that incentivize such behavior.

Because of that, there are a lot of myths about GTA 6 currently floating around the internet. Some come from harmless misunderstandings, while others are more deliberate misrepresentations intended to scare off potential players. To help you navigate the noise, we’ve rounded up some of the most rampant myths currently circulating around GTA 6 and fact-checked them accordingly.

The claim: GTA 6’s story forces you to do chores for Lucia instead of crimes.

If you spent launch day watching reactions to GTA 6’s early hours roll in instead of playing, you might have walked away thinking that Rockstar made a chore simulator. That’s thanks to a few early missions that revolve around Jason getting his home ready for Lucia as she’s about to be released from prison. Players will paint a bedroom for her, fix a leaky roof, and repair some stairs. There’s also an optional quest where players can run errands to prepare for Lucia's arrival, like picking up groceries or buying her a necklace. All of this happens in the first few hours of the game. GTA 6 quickly ramps up after that, getting into the series’ usual flow of cop chases, heists, and shootouts. You can call it a slow start, but know that any mundane missions you’ve seen make up a very small amount of story that you’re likely to see in your very first play session.

The claim: GTA 6 doesn’t allow you to steal cars, or heavily restricts what you can steal.

While there’s a grain of truth to this, it has been heavily exaggerated on social media. There are some select cars that you can’t steal in GTA 6, like those around Jason’s neighborhood or in an NPC’s car lot. But for the most part, you can jack just about any vehicle you see in Leonida. The catch is that you’ll need a device that can copy keys to get into some of the more expensive cars, and you won’t get that until Chapter 3. Being able to steal anything requires some patience as you play through the story, but be rest assured that you can do as much grand theft auto as ever in Grand Theft Auto.

The claim: Airplanes will bounce off of buildings instead of exploding on impact.

This one is a little tricky to unpack because there seem to be two weird things colliding here. After videos of airplanes bouncing off of skyscrapers like rubber began to emerge on social media, players deduced that content creators were sharing videos where they had their Reduced Vehicle Damage setting turned on. It seemed like a textbook case of outrage farming, though there may be a slight bit of truth here. Some players have speculated that GTA 6 may have a few physics bugs that make it tough for certain airliners to blow up as expected. That may be an edge case, but I can confirm that I have crashed plenty of planes into buildings in GTA 6, and they have all exploded into a fiery wreck so far.

The claim: GTA 6 features no autosave, and you will lose progress if you don’t manually save.

When players started reporting that they were losing hours of gameplay because GTA 6 didn’t have an autosave feature, I was very confused. I can open my save file right now and see a dedicated auto save slot that is regularly refreshed as I play. I initially wrote it off as players either lying or not realizing that the auto save only triggers after completing major missions, but it turns out they weren’t hallucinating. GTA 6’s first patch fixed an issue where auto save wasn’t triggering properly. So, yes, GTA 6 does have autosave; it just wasn’t working correctly for some players at launch. It shouldn’t be a problem now, but always remember to save early and often just in case.

The claim: Lucia is cheating on Jason during the story.

This one is downright bizarre. One of the first talking points that came out about GTA 6 was that Jason is a “cuck” who does not realize that Lucia is cheating on him. As someone who has played through the story, I spent days trying to figure out where in the world that blatant lie could be coming from. It turns out it was a good old misinterpretation. Early in the story, Lucia sends a text to an unknown character, which she rushes to hide from Jason when he enters the scene. While some have interpreted that as Lucia having a secret lover, it actually turns out that she was texting a friend from prison. To players’ credit, the scene does feel like it’s built to make you think Lucia is hiding a big secret from Jason, so that reaction might have been exactly what Rockstar was hoping to provoke.

The claim: GTA 6 does not allow you to open fire and kill people in a gay club.

The ugliest rumor to come out of GTA 6 so far is that the game will not allow you to walk into a gay club in Vice City and kill people. There was even a clip going around social media that seemed to support that, sparking some grotesque reactions. The truth is that the location in the video isn’t specifically a gay club. It is a club, and it’s true that you can’t open fire in it, but that’s only because you can’t shoot inside any establishment in GTA 6. This claim would technically be true if there was a gay club in the game, but only as a side effect of the wider systems working the way they do. What is true, though, is that the game features an unkillable non-binary character, according to the actor who portrayed them.

This isn't a moral or ethical issue — boringly, it's about regulation

#3335. 10 Funny Movies To Watch With Your Family This Thanksgiving

Thanksgiving is a time of great football, food, and family. Whether you're gathering with blood relatives or a chosen family, the spirited holiday offers a chance to slow down and reflect on all the things, big and small, to be thankful for. There's nothing better than stuffing yourself with moist turkey, melt-in-your-mouth mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, and freshly baked dinner rolls before camping in front of the TV for a nap (or two) and long-overdue family time with favorite comedies and family-friendly movies.

There are countless holiday movies and TV, including Thanksgiving-themed episodes of The Simpsons, to watch to put you in the mood for gratitude and celebration. Thanksgiving is the perfect time to take time off from work, reconnect with loved ones, and laugh a little.

Millennials will undoubtedly remember Robin Williams' bonkers performance in Les Mayfield's sci-fi comedy Flubber. Through developing a new energy source, Medfield College professor Philip Brainard (Williams) invents a sentient green goo that escapes before flying through the neighborhood. Brainard must recapture it, prove its worth to the college board, and steal back his fiancé, college president Sara Jean Reynolds (Marcia Gay Harden), from his arch nemesis. Slapstick gags and raucous humor characterize this family-friendly gem that has never gotten its proper due.

Williams always dove headfirst into his roles, particularly when it came to comedy. He committed to the bit and delivered knockout performances. As Brainard, he manages to find a tremendous heart pounding at the center of the movie's themes of love and thankfulness.

Director Gurinder Chadha takes cues from National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, but makes the story a tasty Thanksgiving treat. The family gathers for a tremendous feast, but there's naturally plenty of hijinks from various oddball relatives that would give the Griswold family a run for their money. The cast is as star-studded as they come and includes Kyra Sedgwick, Julianna Margulies, and Alfre Woodard.

The hilarious ensemble piece celebrates dysfunctional families (we all have one) and how to find even the smallest things for which to be thankful. What's Cooking? also shines a spotlight on different kinds of families and relationships. It's not only about blood relatives, but a chosen family comes into view, as well.

The Barry Sonnenfeld-directed and starring comedy, Addams Family Values serves as a sequel to 1991's The Addams Family, but it can be viewed on its own without any prior knowledge of the original. For not-yet-inducted family members, Addams Family Values supplies all the macabre, yet good-natured, humor you could want, including an epic scene of Wednesday (Christina Ricci) lighting the set of a camp play on fire.

Joan Cussack joins the cast as Fester's (Christopher Lloyd) new gold-digging wife Debbie Jellinsky, a black widow with a thirst for killing her husbands. In true Addams Family fashion, Values normalizes the strange with smartly written dialogue and funny bone-tickling physicality. It's a guaranteed laugh fest.

Rewatching A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving has been a Thanksgiving tradition for many families for decades - and for good reason. But for those who haven't experienced it yet, Charlie Brown and his friends' antics deliver both humor and thoughtfulness. It's about honoring the holiday through a melodramatic story about Charlie Brown throwing a feast. Naturally, the shenanigans make it a welcome addition to anyone's festivities. And oh yes, the physical football gag is pure cinema.

A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving reminds us to be thankful for the life we've been given, the people who make it worth living, and how we can find a silver lining when things go wrong. Charlie Brown might get exasperated with his friends, but he loves them and wouldn't trade them for the world.

Decidedly not for kids, Donald Petrie's Grumpy Old Men gears its witty, sometimes vulgar, humor for older audiences. Max (Walter Matthau) and John (Jack Lemmon) hate each other, and they've been fighting since 1938. As they've grown older, they've learned to cherish their friendship, oddly enough. They hold grudges, that's to be sure, and will do anything for a good dose of payback. But when things go sideways, health-wise, it becomes clear that they really do care deeply about one another.

Beneath the humor, Grumpy Old Men contains powerful messages about living every day like one's last, cherishing friendships, letting go, and bracing for the future. Matthau and Lemmon expertly offer up performances that capture the humor and heart of the situation. It's also about allowing others into your world when it's the most difficult mountain to climb.

Robin Williams' turn as Alan Parrish in Joe Johnston's Jumanji never gets old. As a child, he discovers a wooden boardgame buried on the site of his father's factory. He takes it home and begins to play, inviting his crush Sarah Whittle (Laura Bell Bundy) to join him. Well, things end horribly with Alan being sucked into the game for decades. Sarah grows into a woman (now played by Bonnie Hunt) afraid of the world and in therapy.

Two kids, Judy (Kiersten Dunst) and Peter (Bradley Pierce), move into the old Parrish house and find the game. They unwittingly unleash giant killer mosquitoes, mischievous monkeys, and a flesh-hungry lion. Oh, and they also free Alan from the game, along with hunter Van Pelt (Jonathan Hyde), who is on a mission to kill him. Dated CGI aside, Jumanji makes you grateful for the cards you've been dealt in life because it could all be worse. What's more, it's one of the best family-friendly movies of the 1990s.

Planes, Trains, and Automobiles stars John Candy and Steve Martin at the top of their game. When Neal (Martin) and Del (Candy) travel home for Thanksgiving, they get a rude awakening when a snowstorm hits the Midwest that prevents them from landing in Chicago. As such, they end up stranded in Wichita, Kansas, and then travel by train and, you guessed it, automobile just to get home to their families. Wackiness leads to an unlikely friendship that makes the film a holiday essential.

A surprising emotional core emerges by the last scene, boosting the already great film into the stratosphere. Planes, Trains, and Automobiles isn't only about the humor but the real heart.

The Muppets doesn't get talked about enough. The comedy musical features all the usual suspects: Kermit the Frog, Miss Piggy, Fozzie the Bear, Animal, and countless others. After parting ways, everyone went off to live their own lives. Some stepped further into the spotlight, while muppets like Kermit retreated into the shadows. Their once-cherished studio has fallen into a derelict state and is being sold to Tex Richman (Chris Cooper), who plans to demolish the property and drill for oil.

When Gary (Jason Segel) takes his girlfriend Mary (Amy Adams) and muppet brother Walter (Peter Linz) to Hollywood, they make a stop at the rundown Muppets studio only to see how tragic it is now. Walter plots to get the band back together in order to raise $10 million in order to save the property from utter destruction. The Muppets is equal parts road trip movie and flashy musical that knows exactly how to tug on the heartstrings, delivering tearful moments aplenty. Of course, it's also characterized by a signature style and humor that make any day truly joyful.

A loose remake of the 1950 movie of the same name, Shawn Levy's Cheaper by the Dozen examines big families, and there's no better time than Thanksgiving to revisit or watch it for the very first time. Steve Martin and Bonnie Hunt play Tom and Kate Baker, heads of a household to a whopping total of 12 children. When Kate launches her book tour, Tom is left to parent all 12 kids without any guidance or know-how on taking care of so many at once. It's a hilarious premise that more than delivers the laughs.

For all big families out there, Cheaper by the Dozen no doubt resonates with its situational humor, particularly when it comes to siblings fighting and a father that can't handle the heat in the kitchen. Once again, Martin knocks it out of the park with his performance, and the cast, which includes pop star Hilary Duff, rises as one of the best comedic ensembles ever.

Jimmy Hayward's 2013 animated movie Free Birds resets Thanksgiving Day as not Turkey Day but Pizza Day. When a smart turkey named Reggie (Owen Wilson) gets selected as the president's pardoned turkey, he enjoys a lavish life of late-night TV and all the pizza he can eat. But a rogue turkey enlists him, or rather kidnaps him, for a top secret mission, and Reggie goes back in time to stop turkeys from being on the menu for Thanksgiving.

Free Birds stars a smorgasbord of big-name talent, including Amy Poehler, Woody Harrelson, Keith David, George Takei, and Dan Fogler, and makes dozens of wisecracking jokes about the game Angry Birds. At the end of the day, who doesn't love a bunch of animated turkeys running around trying to save all turkeys from being eaten on Thanksgiving?

#3334. 'Blade Runner 2099' Creator Reveals the Biggest Challenge for Prime Video’s New Sci-Fi Series

In just a few days, we will be going back to the dystopian future of replicants with a new limited series from Prime Video. Blade Runner 2099 jumps the story forward 50 years and places us in a world where the replicants have finally come out on top and humans have been turned into second-class citizens. The series follows Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human who has gone undercover as a replicant, who works as a blade runner alongside Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a dying replicant in the last days of her life.

Collider got to speak with creator and showrunner Silka Luisa and director Jonathan van Tulleken about this brand new entry into the sci-fi franchise and how the series differentiates itself from the previous two films in the universe. Van Tulleken reveals the films he drew from as reference for the visual palette of the show, and Luisa reveals the process of what it takes to transfer a story into a new format. Luisa also talks about the big change between replicants and humans and how Cora and Olwen's story gives us insight into the new dynamic between the two groups. Finally, she gives some insight into the show's connection to both Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049 and why the show decided to lean away from drawing stronger connections to the previous film.

Going into this, what's the most daunting task when it comes to formulating the world of Blade Runner 2099?

JONATHAN VAN TULLEKEN: I think Silka had written on the page this concept of the sunshine noir, and it was beautiful because Ridley [Scott] described his movie as a 40-year-old movie set 40 years in the future. And [Jordan] Cronenweth had looked to Citizen Kane, his cinematographer, and he described Harrison Ford as a Bogart detective story. And I think, for me, when reading what Silka had written, I was going, "Well, what is our touchstone then? What is our 40 years, 40 years ago?" So I was really thinking of those movies from the 70s and 60s, you know, The French Connection by [William] Friedkin and [Alan J.] Pakula's paranoia trilogy.

What makes those films so connected to what Ridley does as well is they've so much tactility; they're based in vérité. It was where cameras were small enough that you could take them out onto the streets. I think that really led into how we wanted to approach the work, which was something that felt very human, in a way that Ridley's feels so human; it's about what it is to be human, and so we wanted to make it feel human. So we built places that were real; we used original old lights; we used the original glass from the films, the lenses. I think that allowed us to build on what Ridley started and what Denis [Villeneuve] started.

Now the replicants are the ones doing the hunting.

SILKA LUISA: I think just from the narrative perspective, obviously, there's a shift from something that is so cinematic and theatrical. It's a really different experience going into a theater and being locked in a room and letting this world wash over you. We knew we were going to be watching this on TV, and so we really had to consider what is the pace of our Blade Runner? There is a certain tempo to both films that is very meditative; I love it, it puts you in a mindset that is that world, so we were always trying to calibrate both in the writing and in the shooting and ultimately in post when we were editing, how do we pace the show?

Can you have it be this much faster heartbeat? Do you also then need to create moments of breath so that you can actually do the score, which is so iconic? Early on in editing, we had cut the episodes really, really tight just to get that propulsion of Cora's story. But we realized we really needed those breaths because without them, it's not really Blade Runner, and so we were always balancing that.

Talking about the show and the specifics of the narrative, I really like that you flip the script on what we know before, making replicants into Blade Runners who hunt humans. But how did switching the narrative of the story change the approach to how you might structure the story with the focus being on the replicants more than on humans, or at least more than in previous stories?

LUISA: Well, I think the biggest shift was that it was an undercover story. I knew because we were doing a TV show, we would have more time, and that meant that there could be a relationship at the center of the show, not just a single character and their journey. And if you want to tell a relationship story, you know, there's been so many great undercover [stories], that Donnie Brasco dynamic felt like that was going to give you a human and a replicant side-by-side, both of them hiding secrets, that would be really rich terrain.

It's interesting that in this show, you're right, you do have more room to develop things, and you have dual protagonists in the form of Cora and Olwen. Can you talk a little bit about how these two characters have a meeting of the minds as the story progresses? Because Olwen is getting older, she's dying, whereas Cora is forced to go undercover and has to be forced to think more like a replicant.

LUISA: Yeah, at the beginning of the season, both of them are really lacking empathy. Olwen because she's a replicant, and that is just something; without childhoods, they don't develop it in the same way. It's one of the defining characteristics between humans and replicants that we know from the films. And Cora is just a human who is just been stripped of her soul, because sometimes you're in these circumstances where you just are, "Go, go, go," and you can't really take a breath to even think about other people because you just are trying to live the next day. [We] wanted to tell a story of two people who really have lost this fundamental part of what the human experience is, and how can they rediscover it together? Or can they? Can a human and a replicant being side-by-side... can that awaken empathy in both of them?

I'm curious because I know this story does have connections to the original film and 2049. So considering the reveal that we get from 2049 about replicants being able to have children, I was always thinking that in the back of my mind. Why didn't you guys lean into that? Are we going to get more of that, or are there hints trickled throughout the show? Because I have thoughts.

I've seen them all, but I don't want to get too deep into spoilers, but I'm curious about your thoughts on that.

LUISA: Well, I definitely wanted to leave 2049 with enough space to tell their story, because what I love about the end of that film is it felt like it left me wanting more. I could imagine different directions for how all those characters' lives continue, and what it meant for the city, what it meant for them individually, which I think is something that Blade Runner always does. In terms of is the focus on replicants being able to have babies? No, because I feel like that is connected to the 2049 story in such a fundamental way that it felt like touching it would be making decisions for how they were to finish that film.

Blade Runner 2099 premieres November 25 on Prime Video.
