#3298. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 Before Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that users will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting users manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

It blows my mind that there are people out there who choose to go naked with their phones. Between the smooth casing and the constant threat of accidentally dropping my iPhone 18 Pro, going naked gives me way too much anxiety — so I honestly could never bring myself to do it.

That’s why the PhoneBack by Süti immediately caught my eye. Rather than wrapping my iPhone 18 Pro in a silicone or polycarbonate shell that adds bulks to its size, it’s a minimalist magnetic backplate that protects the rear — while also sprinkling a little of style at the same time. For someone like me who refuses to go caseless, it’s easily the closest alternative I’d be willing to go to achieve that naked iPhone look. Here’s why.

Do you hate bulky cases? Well, the Süti PhoneBack is one of the easiest, most efforless iPhone cases around since it snaps onto the back via MagSafe to protect the back glass and camera bump. At just 2.34 mm thin, it adds welcome grip and lets you swap styles, all without adhesives or blocking wireless charging.

What I really love about the PhoneBack is how clever it is at delivering just enough protection against everyday wear and tear, all while completely preserving the "naked" look and feel of the iPhone 18 Pro. Since it relies on a MagSafe connection, it takes seconds to snap directly onto the back — and it beats having to deal with the headaches of installing one of those adhesive vinyl skins.

Best of all, the PhoneBack by Süti gives me a quick and effortless way to change the colors or textures whenever the mood strikes, unlike a permanent wrap that’s notoriously difficult to peel off.

Options range from soft-touch Silicone that I feel is more scratch-resistant, the two-tone look of the iCandy cases, to my favorite NanoLeather one that adds texture to the back of my iPhone 18 Pro. One of the downsides of upgrading from the iPhone 17 Pro to the 18 Pro is that the former’s signature Cosmic Orange color isn’t available, but I’m able to easily emulate that look with the orange silicone PhoneBack.

Even though the Süti PhoneBack uses magnets to snap onto my iPhone, it doesn't get in the way of wireless charging at all. That’s because it packs a neodymium magnet array, which still lets me drop the phone right onto a MagSafe or Qi2 charging pad without ever pulling the backplate off. On top of that, I can keep using my favorite MagSafe accessories — like magnetic wallets, desk stands, car mounts, power banks, and more.

I’ll say it again: the Süti PhoneBack is hands down the closest I’ll ever get to rocking a naked iPhone 18 Pro. It strikes that balance I want with its minimalist design, extra grip, and effortless customization — all without sacrificing MagSafe charging or accessory support. That said, I still have to be very careful because it leaves the sides and front glass completely exposed. If you want full 360-degree drop protection, stick with a traditional case. But if you crave that bare-metal feel in hand and just want scratch protection and a fresh look for the back, the PhoneBack is tough to beat.

#3294. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

And it incorporates a very important football game, so it actually ties in with my second pick of the week, Netflix's NFL gameday.

On the eve of Thanksgiving, Netflix will be the place to watch the Packers vs. Rams. Both teams have identical records this season, so it could be a closely contested matchup. And if football isn’t for you, how about the return of a Netflix original drama that explores an even more cutthroat world than professional athletics: an upper-society clique in East Texas.

Why you should watch it: “The Mosquito Bowl’s” focus on the brutality of WWII, camaraderie, and the sacrifices made by ordinary people — each member of the quartet effectively gives up their athletic dreams to enlist — is not new for the genre, but they’re worthwhile topics, and this Netflix original should still be an emotionally impactful watch.

#3289. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

#3287. Fair Isle Sweaters Can Be Tricky to Style: Here's How to Pull It Off

The traditional knit might feel tricky or even intimidating to style, but these easy denim and skirt pairings make it a clear winter outfit staple.

Some might say the Fair Isle sweaters only look good during Thanksgiving week. We are brave enough to disagree with this warm (and cozy) take. In our book, we need a little alpine charm in our life every single day this winter. How else could we keep ourselves from freezing during the coldest temperatures?

Fair Isle sweaters are a traditional knitting style that features a distinctive pattern with multiple colors—either bold or neutral shades. The most trendy pattern we're seeing right now is geometric styles around the neckline or the center of the sweater. Still, even though it's adorable and cozy, this type of sweater might seem difficult to style.

Luckily, we've got you covered. No need to freeze in front of your closet when getting dressed in the morning! And the best part? Carve Designs has the chic Fair Isle sweaters and the styles to pair it with on sale for 25% off, just in time for Black Friday.

So, keep scrolling to see how we'd recommend pairing this (apparently) controversial and traditional sweater.

1. The most popular way to style the Fair Isle sweaters is with jeans. It's a no-brainer. You can style it more casually with relaxed boyfriend jeans or light-wash barrel jeans, paired with boots or sneakers. It can also feel dressier with a dark wide-leg jean, styled with gold jewelry, heels, and a chic shoulder bag—while keeping that cozy comfort with the trendy pattern.

2. If you want to make your outfit a little more interesting (but still casual), the Fair Isle sweater can also be styled with this pair of corduroy pants. This pairing adds an extra layer of textural and color difference to pop against the cozy pattern of the sweater. Add a pair of brown boots or cozy clogs to keep the working vibe going.

3. Skirts are an easy way to put a classy outfit together, especially during the fall season (but even during the winter, skirts can be layered over fleece tights to keep you warm). We recommend opting for a maxi skirt and pairing it with knee-high boots—either a silky one in a light color or a dark-wash denim one.

4. Wearing sweaters by themselves can look a little too plain for some personal styles out there, even with the Fair Isle pattern. An easy way to create some interest on the top half of your outfit is to layer a button-down with a collar under your sweater—pick between a silkier texture, like this Angela Kindsilk Top, or a more structured one, like this western denim style one.

Made from a blend of merino wool, recycled nylon, and alpaca, this sweater adds a little alpine charm to your outfit, with its oversized fit, raglan sleeves, hi-low hem, and chunky design.

I'm Erin, and welcome to The Coffee Lab Episode 25, the series where we forget coffee snobbery. The Coffee Lab is all about making coffee fun. Join me as I help you kickstart your coffee journey!

Here at The Coffee Lab, I'm always chomping at the bit to try out the newest and most exciting innovations in the coffee world. This episode is no different: Sage (that's Breville for all you U.S. folk) invited me to its London headquarters to try out the brand-new Barista Express Neo.

The original Barista Express was released in 2009 — and I don't think it's dramatic to say this espresso machine changed the home coffee game. As Breville also owns Baratza, the Barista Express has a high(enough)-quality Baratza grinder like the Baratza Encore ESP. On top of that, it's got all of Breville's iconic coffee-snob-approved features like a PID controller and customizable pre-infusion.

So what does the new Barista Express Neo bring to the party? One majorly impressive, unprecedented feature: SmoothSip. Right, but what can SmoothSip actually do? What does this mean for the future of coffee? I've got all the answers for you.

Although only available in the U.K. right now, the Breville/Sage Barista Express Neo is one of the coffee scene's most exciting new arrivals. With the patented SmoothSip technology, dialling in is a thing of the past.

In short, SmoothSip is a built-in pressure controller that ensures espresso will always come out of the portafilter. That's it.

Grind too fine? SmoothSip will increase pressure to get some coffee out.

Grind too coarse? SmoothSip will reduce pressure to slow down the espresso.

Of course, this isn't the machine for genuine coffee snobs. If you laugh at the idea of a built-in grinder, let alone extracting espresso at anything other than the optimal 9 bars of pressure, you'd be better off with the iconic Bambino Plus ($499) or even the heat-exchanger Lelit Mara X3 ($1,999).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

And after extraction, the machine tells you which grind setting to use so your next shot is closer to "perfect".

Yes, increasing or lowering pressure during extraction does affect the taste of espresso. This machine isn't for people who would class themselves as coffee snobs, and that's okay. If we were all the same, life would be boring, and there would be one brand of espresso machine for everyone in the world.

However, I drank enough espresso during the Breville event that I got the caffeine shakes, and I don't drink bad-tasting coffee. So take from that what you will!

As I write this, I haven't reviewed the Breville Barista Express Neo yet. It only came out three days ago, and it's not even available in the U.S. yet. It's still early days.

Even so, I have tried the Barista Express Neo's espresso. I tried an underextracted (ground too coarse) espresso made on the Barista Express and the Neo, and the Neo's shot tasted much better. Of course, it was still a little sour, but it was ten times more palatable than the Barista Express's acidic shot.

I made one flat white on the Neo, but this is nowhere near enough for me to write the comprehensive review. I usually make upwards of twenty flat whites on each machine during testing, with a whole horde of guinea pigs to give me feedback.

So please stay tuned for my full review, which will probably come in the new year. I'm so excited to test the Breville Barista Express Neo. It's one of the most exciting espresso machines of the year.

#3281. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

Holy triceps! These three moves test your upper-body strength for Hollywood-worthy arms. I don't know about you, but I've loved seeing Khloé Kardashian's fitness journey evolve over the years, and how she's inspired other women to lift heavy and get strong.

We already know the benefits of lifting weights, from improving strength and body composition to supporting bone health, cardiovascular health, mental well-being and body confidence. The more women following in Khloé's footsteps, the better, I say.

While researching Khloé, I came across her arm routine with her trainer, Joel Bouraima, and I had to share. Khloé used to hate her arms, but hate no more. She's now “really proud” of herself. "I'm a strength training girl,” she says. “I love to see definition, and I love to know that I'm filling up my skin. I can't explain it, but that makes me feel really good.”

A post shared by Lucy Miller (@lucycmiller_)

Khloé Kardashian reportedly turns up 30 minutes early for her workouts to stretch and mobilize, even when they start at 6 a.m. Her coach says she works for an hour a day, Monday through Friday, fitting her training around the school run. As a single mom of two, she doesn’t have “a celebrity schedule with unlimited time.”

Her trainer also points to consistency and preparation as Khloé's real advantages. He's trained her since 2013, and despite years of regular sessions, she admits she's still learning.

“I've been doing this for 100 years, and I still don't know what does what,” she joked during the workout as the pair discussed which exercises worked which muscles. But her journey hasn't always been about confidence. Khloé also revealed that a comment from a previous female trainer about her arms has stayed with her for years.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

“I've never forgotten those words about my arms. I always think I'm a work in progress,” she says. And we couldn't agree more.

Here are three exercises from her arm workout, and why they're worth adding to your own strength routine. You’ll need access to a cable machine or a resistance band if you don’t have a cable, and some dumbbells.

Targets: Shoulders, particularly the lateral deltoids

Why it works: Cable lateral raises target the muscles along the sides of your shoulders, helping build strength and definition. Unlike dumbbells, cables provide resistance throughout all of the movement, challenging your shoulders as you lift and lower your arm.

When I tried it: This move is relatively easy to set up, and using the cable means you have resistance on the way up and the way down. I've never bent over to do a lateral raise before, but by doing this, I could feel the emphasis shift toward the posterior deltoids (rear shoulder muscles), with help from my traps and triceps, too.

Targets: Shoulders, particularly the lateral deltoids.

Why it works: Dumbbell lateral raises are a simple but effective way to strengthen your shoulders. By lifting the weights out to your sides, you target the lateral deltoids, which help give your shoulders their rounded shape. Better still, all you need is a pair of dumbbells.

When I tried it: I loved how much this move isolates the shoulders, really giving them that nice burn and helping build a strong, athletic shape. It's one of those exercises that looks relatively simple, but you certainly feel it when doing it.

Why it works: Shoulder presses are a compound exercise, meaning they work several muscle groups at once. They strengthen your shoulders and triceps while also challenging your core to keep you stable, helping build the upper-body strength needed for everyday lifting and reaching.

When I tried it: The shoulder press is a great move for building strong, defined shoulders, working the anterior and lateral heads of the deltoids. I like to go heavy with this move, and if I need to use my legs to help me get the last few reps up, then so be it. I love the look of strong shoulders.

“The way we target the muscles in her arms is very localized and specific,” Joel shares.

“We often use specific hand grips to target different parts of the arms. For example, with the biceps, we use a hammer grip to avoid developing the short part of the biceps; the part that gives you the bump, which Khloé doesn't want.”

“I love to see definition,” says Khloé, “and each time I see any muscle lines or definition, I think I did that… it's been years in the making. It doesn't just happen overnight,” she says. “Muscle is hard to get.”

And you don't need a celebrity trainer to follow suit. Just commit and stick to “efficiency, intensity and longevity,” says Joel.

#3277. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

The Shark PowerDetect Transformer has actually convinced me to ditch my cordless stick in favour of this corded upright. This is no ordinary upright either; it’s 3-in-1, so it transforms effortlessly from an upright into a stick and handheld cleaner at the touch of a button. It also has automatic floor and dirt detection, powerful suction, and a clever self-emptying system. However, its weight and trailing cord could make whole-home cleaning a little more complicated.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I have tested a lot of the best vacuum cleaners over the years. From corded uprights to cordless lightweight stick models. Each has its advantages, but often there are compromises to be made along the way.

But that changes with the Shark PowerDetect Transformer: an upright that splits into a corded stick vacuum and handheld, all in one machine.

Shark has also packed in the technology with this vacuum. Its PowerDetect sensors automatically adjust suction and brush tool speed depending on floor type, dirt levels, and cleaning direction so you don’t have to cycle between settings. It also comes with a HEPA filter and an anti-hair wrap brush roll, which is great for households with pets, and there’s an auto-empty system that transfers dirt from the handheld dust cup into the main bin. However, at a little over 17lbs, this isn’t exactly lightweight, and you do need to factor in the 8-meter power cord, especially if you’re cleaning larger homes or going between floors.

But is it enough to convince you to ditch the convenience of cordless and go back to corded? Find out what happened when I put it to work.

The Shark PowerDetect Transformer was launched in September 2026 and retails for $649.99/£499.99 at SharkNinja or selected retailers like Amazon UK, Amazon US, Curry’s and Best Buy.

It comes in two colors, Midnight Steel and Sagewood, although if you're in the UK and want the Sagewood you'll need to get it from Amazon as Shark don't stock that color.

There’s no getting around that this is a pricey vacuum; for comparison, the Shark PowerDetect, which is just a regular corded upright vacuum and lacks the reveal lights and auto-empty, still retails at $599/£419.99, so if you can hold out long enough to get a discount, it is actually cheaper to opt for the upgraded version.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The question is whether the three-in-one design really offers enough convenience to make that higher price tag worth it.

If you already own a handheld or stick vacuum, then the Transformer may feel like an expensive way to add an upright vacuum to the list, especially when you consider that the Shark Classic Upright is priced at just $379.99 / £219.99, which is reduced to £129.99 at sale price for UK buyers.

In terms of non-Shark alternatives, the Dyson Ball Animal 3 is the most obvious comparison. This corded vacuum is suitable for all floor types and has a telescopic handle which rotates in three directions for 360º cleaning. It’s even cheaper than the Shark, priced at $499 / £329.99, but you do miss out on the HEPA filter, reveal lights, and smart sensors.

Honestly, there’s nothing quite like the Shark PowerDetect currently on the market unless you’re willing to make some sacrifices in terms of features and functions.

When you first look at the Shark PowerDetect Transformer, you’ll be forgiven for thinking it looks like just a regular upright vacuum.

But look a little closer, and you’ll see that the design is actually the thing that makes this cleaner stand apart.

It uses a modular design that can transform it from an upright to a stick to a handheld, all with the click of a button.

Shark isn’t a stranger to the idea of modular upright vacuum cleaners. The PowerDetect Powered LiftAway is another good example where the main unit detaches, allowing you to effortlessly switch between different cleaning modes.

However, that model retains the traditional hose design, whereas the PowerDetect Transformer does away with the hose altogether for a much smoother and more flexible experience.

It’s a weird vacuum to describe, because when it is fully together, it’s not the smallest or lightest machine, measuring 46.3 x 11.2 x 12.5 inches and weighing over 17lbs.

But when you pop off the wand for the stick and handheld functions, it suddenly becomes very light and flexible, so it’s a bit of an odd hybrid of a vacuum cleaner in that it’s heavy and bulky whilst being lightweight all at the same time.

The controls are extremely uncomplicated. There’s an on/off button at the top of the machine; this is all you really need, as that will set the vacuum straight into auto mode. However, if you do feel like you want a little more control, there is also a mode button which will allow you to toggle between eco, detect, and boost.

Personally, this machine does a great job of detecting what type of floor you’re vacuuming and the level of dirt it can detect, so I’d just leave it on auto every time to ensure you’re getting the best clean.

You get plenty of accessories with this vacuum, including a duster crevice tool, stair tool, HairPro pet power brush and an anti-allergen dusting brush. The main floor head uses a dual-roller system which uses Anti-Hair wrap technology, so ideal if you have pets or you’re like me and shed more than the dogs.

Another interesting design point for this vacuum is that it has two bins, there’s the main bin, which is a very generous 1.3 litres, but then there’s also a smaller 0.2L bin, which is used when in handheld mode and the great thing is that when you reattach it, the smaller bin self-empties into the main bin so you don’t have to empty the bin twice. Of course, this vacuum is corded so you don’t quite have the same convenience you do when it comes to cordless but with an 8-meter cord, it does cover quite a lot of ground before you run out of wire.

This vacuum comes in two colorways, Midnight Steel and Sage, which is more interesting than the typical black or grey look most vacuums have. The colours give it a distinct look without being too flashy, and whilst it’s not exactly a piece of home decor you’d actively want on display, it certainly doesn’t look hideous if you don’t have anywhere to store it when not in use.

In my opinion, this is a really well-built vacuum; the plastics are thick and don’t feel as though they’re going to break after heavy use. The attachments secure well, although surprisingly they don’t click in, so it can be a bit of a struggle to pull them out if you want to reattach the wand or change attachments. The buttons to release the bin and the wand are easy to push; they don’t feel too stiff. The build quality feels as though this is a good choice for busy households, as it’s certainly robust enough to withstand knocks and bashes of family life.

To assess the Shark PowerDetect Transformer’s cleaning performance, I ran a number of tests on a range of flooring, including hard floors, long-pile carpet, and short-pile carpet. I used seeds, Rice Krispies, and hair on each surface to see how much the vacuum cleaner picked up.

Straight off the bat, I was super impressed by the performance of the Shark PowerDetect Transformer. I thought my floors were clean before I started using this vacuum, and to say I was a bit shocked is an understatement.

The PowerDetect Transformer uses a DuoClean Detect floorhead, which has two brushrolls that have been designed to tackle a range of different flooring.

This is ideal if you have a mixture of flooring types throughout your home, as it automatically detects the surface it’s working on and adjusts the suction and speed accordingly. I thought this particularly useful, especially when vacuuming downstairs where I have carpet, hard floors, and tiles.

I’ve been using a Dyson V12 Absolute for the last couple of years in conjunction with a robot vacuum, so I didn’t think there could possibly be much dirt and debris left in my carpets. But from the first use of this vacuum, my carpets instantly looked cleaner and the amount of dust and fur that found its way inside of the dust bin was quite frankly insane.

The vacuum uses sensors to identify areas where additional cleaning power is needed. Once it detects those areas, it increases the suction and speed at which it works.

I’ve tested enough vacuum cleaners over the years to have heard all these marketing claims before, so I wasn’t too convinced this would be a feature that I noticed, but I was really blown away by just how well it worked. Especially around the areas where my dogs’ beds are kept.

These, of course, are some of the dirtier spots in the house, but when going over those areas, the vacuum LED went purple, which signified a dirty area and the power increased. It’s a really useful feature, especially if you have pets, because it means you don’t have to practice guesswork by repeatedly going over the same areas.

The reveal lighting is another welcome addition, especially when vacuuming the wood and tiled floor. It did a great job of showing up dog hair on the floor, which I couldn’t see at all when the light wasn’t illuminating it. It’s one of those features that you may not think you really need until you see it in action and then you can’t do without it.

This is a really nice vacuum to manoeuvre around. It gets up close to the edges so the whole floor really does feel like it’s had a good clean. However, because of the size of the bin, if you’re hoping to get underneath furniture like sofas, you may struggle.

You can of course, use it as a stick vacuum, but then you don’t have a large head to be able to cover a large area, so there is a little bit of a problem there.

Whilst the PowerDetect Transformer isn’t specifically a pet vacuum, it’s a great choice if you do have pets. The Shark Anti-Hair Wrap technology means that hair doesn’t get tangled around the brush rolls.

This isn’t just relevant to pets either; my hair gets everywhere, and my Dyson always needs the hair cut away from the brush. I’ve been using this vacuum for a couple of months now, and not once have I had to cut my hair from the roll, so it really does work.

There’s also a HairPro pet power brush included, which is for upholstery and other areas where pet hair accumulates. I thought this did a great job of getting rid of dog hair on the sofa, but I didn’t really rate it when doing the stairs; it didn’t quite get into the edges to pick up the fur that had accumulated, so I still had to manually brush it down first.

As for the collection, the 1.3-litre dustbin is incredibly generous. I have seven rooms in total in my house and I empty it after each clean, it isn’t full to the top but it is pretty full so you can certainly do a full clean through the house without having to stop and empty the bin every five minutes.

The smaller 0.2 litre bin that is attached to the handheld section is ok, I find the limit is just doing the stairs with it before I need to empty it into the main bin, so if you’re planning on doing any areas that are heavily soiled, you may have to empty midway through the job which could get a little annoying after a while.

You can open and empty the small bin manually if you want, but to activate the self-emptying you just have to re-dock the wand onto the main body, so if you’re finished with cleaning, it makes more sense to just do it that way.

This Shark does have a HEPA filter, and also the bin has an Anti-Allergen complete seal, so it catches and traps dust within the bin rather than pushing them back into the room. This makes it a great choice for anyone with allergies, but it’s also good to know that your hard work won’t be undone by emptying the bin.

One thing that’s worth noting is the weight. At a little over 17lbs, this isn’t a very lightweight vacuum when being used as an upright, so if you are going to move it between floors, then it’s worth just thinking about. However, the powered floorhead means that it’s light and easy to move across carpets; I certainly don’t feel like I’ve done a workout when I’ve finished vacuuming.

The Shark PowerDetect Transformer performed well on hard flooring. The built-in reveal lights do a good job of highlighting any dust and fur that can’t be seen by the naked eye. The head also glides around the flooring with ease and the auto-detect did a great job of recognising when the vacuum was going from hardwood to vinyl to tiles.

Vacuuming up the Rice Krispies and the seeds was ideal, it didn’t crush anything, just sucked it up in one go, making the job quick and easy. Nothing got pushed out to the sides either so it didn’t spread it across the floor.

This vacuum does incredibly well on carpeted floor. It's powerful suction gets deep in to the fibres and removes dust, debris, pet hair and anything else that may be hanging around. I was blown away how easily the vacuum picked up the test products. The Rice Krispies especially as they didn't get crushed to smashed in to the carpet, the moment the vacuum went over the top, it just sucked them up. It didn't have any problems picking up the chia seeds either which are small and could have easily been lost within the fibres but it vacuumed it all up leaving none behind. It was really interesting when it came to vacuuming up the hair as it also took in more debris that it found, and that was after the floor had already been vacuumed, so if there's anything on your carpet, this vacuum is going to suck it up.

Noise-wise, I don’t think this vacuum is over the top loud, I used the Decibel X app around 3 feet away from the vacuum and it recorded a reading of 71.1dB whilst it was cleaning.

If people are working or relaxing nearby, then it could be distracting, but it certainly isn’t the loudest vacuum that I’ve tested.

Despite being a three-in-one vacuum, the Shark PowerDetect Transformer doesn’t really need much space. It’s not the smallest vacuum, measuring 46.3 x 11.2 x 12.5 inches.

But one advantage of it being a corded model is that it can be kept in its upright configuration and doesn’t need to be attached to the wall, placed on a charging dock, or be anywhere near a power outlet. I’ve stored mine under the stairs, and there’s plenty of room.

Shark has made some effort to think about how to store the accessories too. It ships with a bag so you can keep the additional tools together if you don’t want to risk them getting lost. But it also comes with some clips which create onboard accessory storage if you’d rather keep them with the unit. There are also dedicated hooks to keep the power cable tidy.

Maintenance is also pretty straightforward. The bin is bagless, so there’s no need to buy replacement bags. The bin also detaches from the main unit so you can take it outside directly to the bin to empty. You will want to clean the dust bin, as, speaking from my own experience, it does get very dusty. The bin lid opens from the bottom and the top so it’s easy to get a cloth in there and give it a good clean.

The vacuum does have multiple filters, which are washable and require a little more maintenance. The filters are really easy to get out; they just pull out from their area, so there’s no real issue with removing them.

As with most upright Shark vacuums, there is an anti-odor cartridge at the front of the floor head. This keeps things smelling fresh when the vacuum is running and needs to be replaced every six months. These cost $7.99/£7.99 direct from SharkNinja, but you can buy off-brand versions if you prefer.

Overall, this isn’t a machine that you’re going to have to spend a lot of time maintaining. But it is important to keep it clean and tidy so that you get the best performance out of it throughout its lifetime.

The Shark PowerDetect Transformer is an impressive upright cleaner, and you don’t have to compromise on the convenience of a stick or handheld.

To say that this vacuum cleaner leaves nothing behind is an understatement. It performed consistently well across all three surfaces, collecting almost all of the test items that I laid down for it.

It brings together an innovative design with a powerful performance that’s enough to convince me to ditch my cordless stick and go all in on this corded upright. I was really impressed by how well this vacuum got to work on carpets. It lifted embedded fur and dust that I had no idea was even there. I also found that being able to switch between different cleaning configurations made giving the house a full deep clean a lot easier.

There are a couple of drawbacks, of course: being corded means it’s not so easy to just grab it and vacuum up any small spills because you have to consciously get it out and plug it in. Also moving between floors is also a bit of a pain, again you have to carry it about.

However, when you consider that I managed to vacuum the whole house in under 20 minutes, that’s a pretty good indication that this vacuum does a great job quickly.

For anyone looking for the cleaning power of an upright with the flexibility of a stick and handheld vacuum, the Shark PowerDetect Transformer is a brilliant option.

#3272. Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3269. How to Cancel Your Amazon Prime Membership After Black Friday and Cyber Monday

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

One of Amazon’s biggest sales of the year, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, is set to start Nov. 27, but many early deals are already rolling in. To take advantage of everything the sale has to offer, you’re going to need to be a Prime Member. If you sign up for an Amazon Prime account to take advantage of the sale but decide you don’t want to pay for an ongoing membership, you’ll need to cancel your subscription before the end of your free trial.

You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

#3268. Major privacy breaches reported in Muse AI – company responds [U]

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user …

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”

Muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Update: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

"AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta has taken issue with the messaging claims. It says that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

With Android, users have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The company also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

#3265. Canva introduces new controls to hide generative AI features

In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today announced new controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The company notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:

The company says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between users with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two new controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating new content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything new. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the company’s design content library, Canva said that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

#3262. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3261. OLED iMac plans may be cancelled by Apple for two reasons

Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited …

1. The size. 24” is undesirable at the prices they ask.

2. No target display mode. Making the display unusable with multiple computers or after you’ve upgraded to a new model of Mac.

Adding OLED doesn’t solve either of these, and raising the price obviously doesn’t solve it.

At the same time, there’s an important distinction between commercial viability and margins. Apple is concerned with the latter, not the former.

An OLED iMac would be a commercially viable product at current prices, but it might not have the 30 to 40 % hardware profit margins they desire. Adding OLED would raise Apples costs, without adding more sales (due to 1 and 2) to offset that slightly lower but (still industry leading) profit margin.

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The company subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

It was expected that the company would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

The company is said to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […]

The biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision.

The report suggests that incoming CEO John Ternus has been reviewing the commercial viability of upgrading more products to OLED. As further evidence, the report says Apple has sent quotation requests to LCD suppliers for an iMac screen to be launched in around 2029.
